posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What an Agent Actually Sees
posts.subtitle: Prompt engineering picks the words; context engineering picks what's in the window at all
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what goes into an agent's context window on every turn — system prompt, tools, retrieved data, and history — instead of just how it's phrased. As agents run longer and call more tools, the bottleneck shifts from prompt wording to context curation: what to load just-in-time, what to compact, and what to hand off to a sub-agent with its own clean window.

slides.title: The Window Is the Bottleneck, Not the Wording
slides.body: A single-shot chatbot lives or dies by prompt phrasing. A multi-step agent lives or dies by what's still in its context window on turn 40 — and most of what's in there by then isn't the system prompt.

slides.title: Long Agent Runs Drown Their Own Context
slides.body: Every tool call, file read, and sub-task result gets appended to the transcript. Left unmanaged, that transcript grows until it crowds out the instructions that actually matter.
bullets: A coding agent that greps a large repo can accumulate tens of thousands of tokens of file contents in a few turns — most of it irrelevant by the time it's needed again
Attention degrades over long, cluttered contexts (context rot): the model still 'sees' early instructions but weighs them less as noise piles up
Redundant or stale tool outputs increase both cost and latency without adding information
More tools in the system prompt means more candidates to misuse — tool-selection errors climb with an unpruned toolbox

slides.title: Four Levers: Prompt, Tools, Retrieval, Compaction
slides.body: Context engineering isn't one trick — it's a set of decisions made fresh on every turn about what earns a place in a finite window.
bullets: System prompt altitude: specific enough to be actionable, general enough to not hard-code brittle logic — the same failure mode as over-fitted few-shot prompts
Tool curation: ship the minimal set of non-overlapping tools for the current task, not every tool the agent could ever need

Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references (file paths, doc IDs) in context and load full content only when a step actually needs it, mirroring how a human keeps a file system instead of memorizing every file
Compaction: summarize or discard stale turns before they push out live information, preserving decisions and open threads while dropping raw tool output that's already been used

slides.title: A Scratchpad Survives What the Context Window Doesn't
slides.body: Long-horizon agents externalize state instead of trusting it to stay in the window. A persistent note file acts as memory that outlives compaction.
bullets: Agent writes key facts (file locations, decisions made, remaining steps) to a NOTES.md or task-state file as it works
When context is compacted or a sub-agent finishes, the note file — not the transcript — is the source of truth for what happened
Sub-agents get a clean, narrow context window scoped to one piece of work, then return only a condensed result to the parent's window
This trades some coordination overhead (writing/reading notes costs tokens too) for a context budget that doesn't grow unbounded

slides.title: Same Task, Two Context Strategies
slides.body: A coding agent is asked to fix a bug in a 400-file repo.
bullets: Context-stuffing approach: agent greps broadly and pastes every plausibly-related file into context up front — 60K+ tokens before it writes a single line, and the actual bug is buried between two unrelated files

Context-engineered approach: agent starts with just file names and a directory tree, greps for the specific error string, opens only the 2-3 files that match, and notes 'bug is in auth/session.py:142, cause: expired token not refreshed' before making the edit
The second run finishes with a fraction of the tokens spent and a note trail that lets it resume correctly even if the session is compacted mid-fix

slides.title: Context-Stuffed vs. Context-Engineered Agents

rows: Low, scales with what's actually needed
Extra tool round-trips, but smaller prefill
Loses state when transcript is summarized

slides.title: When Context Engineering Backfires
slides.body: These techniques add moving parts, and moving parts fail in their own ways.
bullets: Over-aggressive compaction can silently drop a constraint the agent needed three steps later — summarization is lossy by definition
Just-in-time retrieval adds real latency: extra tool calls to fetch what could have been loaded once, which hurts on short, simple tasks
Sub-agent isolation can lose shared context the parent needed — a sub-agent that 'fixes' one file without knowing a sibling file depends on its interface
For short tasks with small, stable data, a big context window plus prompt caching is simpler and cheaper than building retrieval/compaction machinery

slides.title: Treat the Context Window Like Scarce Memory
bullets: Prompt engineering optimizes what you say; context engineering optimizes what's even in the room
Load just-in-time, not just-in-case — references beat pasted content until the content is actually needed
Externalize state to a scratchpad/notes file so long runs survive compaction and sub-agent handoffs
It's an added cost, not a default — reach for it when tasks are long-horizon and tool-heavy, not for short single-turn calls

questions.prompt: What is the main failure mode that 'context rot' describes?
options: The model runs out of API credits mid-task
The model technically still has early instructions in context but weighs them less as clutter accumulates
The context window physically deletes old tokens after a fixed time limit
The model refuses to process contexts longer than its training data
questions.explanation: Context rot isn't about hitting a hard token limit — it's that attention over a long, cluttered context degrades, so instructions from early in the conversation get effectively deprioritized even though they're still technically present.

questions.prompt: Why do long-horizon agents write to an external notes/scratchpad file instead of relying only on the transcript?
options: It's required by most LLM APIs for tool calling to work
It makes the model's responses faster to generate
It preserves key state (decisions, remaining steps) across compaction or sub-agent handoffs, where the raw transcript can't be trusted to survive
It reduces the number of tools the agent needs
questions.explanation: Compaction summarizes or drops old turns, and sub-agents return only condensed results to the parent. A notes file gives the agent a durable source of truth that doesn't depend on the transcript staying intact.

questions.prompt: When is context engineering LEAST worth the added complexity?
options: A multi-hour agent run over a large, changing codebase with many tool calls
A short, single-turn task over small, stable data where a big context window and prompt caching already work fine
An agent that spawns many sub-agents to parallelize research
A task where the transcript is likely to be compacted multiple times
questions.explanation: Just-in-time retrieval and compaction add tool round-trips and lossy summarization — real costs. For short tasks with small, stable inputs, simply keeping everything in a large cached context window is cheaper and simpler.

posts.title: VideoCoCo: Simulate the Physics Before You Render It
posts.subtitle: An agent writes executable Blender code as its chain-of-thought so video generation stops faking gravity
posts.summary: VideoCoCo has a coding agent write an executable Blender program as a process-level chain-of-thought before any pixel is generated, producing a deterministic 'clay proxy' video that gets the physics right, then restyling that proxy into a photorealistic clip. On PhyGenBench and VBench-2.0 it beats its OmniWeaving baseline and the strongest open text-to-video baselines by a wide margin, though it's still validated on a small, hand-checked set of physical phenomena.

slides.title: Text-to-video models don't know what gravity is
slides.body: VideoCoCo (Li, Ren, Ma, et al.) argues that text-to-video models fail at physics not because they lack scale, but because they're asked to infer an entire scene's temporal evolution from a few compressed words — with no explicit model of state anywhere in the pipeline.

slides.title: Chain-of-thought for video has been non-executable so far
slides.body: Prior attempts to add reasoning to video generation insert intermediate plans or sketch frames as a CoT step — but those representations are either not executable or too temporally sparse to actually control the full spatiotemporal process.
bullets: A melting ice cube, a boiling pot, or a buoyant object floating all require causal state that unfolds over time — you can't fake that with a text prompt alone
A caption like 'ice melts in water' tells a model the destination, not the mechanism — nothing enforces that displaced water rises as the cube shrinks
Sketch-based or keyframe-based CoT still leaves the model to interpolate physics between sparse anchors, which is exactly where errors creep back in

slides.title: Make the chain-of-thought a program that actually runs
slides.body: VideoCoCo's coding agent writes a Blender program from the prompt — real simulation code with mass, forces, and collisions — and an execution engine runs it to produce a neutral white/clay proxy video that captures correct motion and causality through shape and deformation, deliberately stripped of color and texture.
bullets: The proxy is 'physically correct but visually boring' by design — geometry and motion are locked in before style enters the pipeline
A verification step checks the proxy against the physical plan for causality: a caused state (water rising) must stay hidden until its causing transition (cube sinking) actually happens
Only after the proxy passes verification does a generative video engine restyle it into a photorealistic clip via draft-conditioned editing

slides.title: A three-stage, agentic dual-engine pipeline
slides.body: The system pairs a deterministic simulation engine (for the physics-correct draft) with a generative video engine (for photorealism), coordinated by an agent through five reusable 'Agent Skills.'
bullets: Stage 1 — Code planning: agent synthesizes Blender code specifying the scene and its full temporal evolution
Stage 2 — Deterministic draft: the simulation engine executes that code into a clay-proxy video, then checks it for causal consistency
Stage 3 — Photorealistic restyle: a video-editing model transforms the verified proxy into the final clip using per-case edit instructions, without touching the underlying motion

slides.title: It beats its own baseline and the strongest open model
slides.body: VideoCoCo posts the best per-category PhyGenBench scores in mechanics (0.558), optics (0.613), and material (0.525) — the categories most likely to expose a model 'faking' physics with texture tricks instead of real motion.

slides.title: Worked example: a melting ice cube in water
slides.body: This is one of the eight hand-checked toy cases in VideoCoCo's public dataset, covering buoyancy, stress/deformation, melting, surface tension, sublimation, elasticity, and boiling.
bullets: A plain T2V model given 'ice cube melts in a glass of water' has to hallucinate the whole sequence from that one sentence — it often shrinks the cube uniformly with no displaced water and no thermal gradient
VideoCoCo's agent instead writes simulation code with an actual thermal-melt model and buoyant force on the shrinking solid

The clay-proxy stage locks in correct water displacement and cube deformation before any photorealistic texture is applied — so the final restyled clip inherits physics that were verified, not generated

slides.title: Where it breaks down
slides.body: The pipeline is only as physically correct as the code the agent writes — and it adds real cost before a single video frame appears.
bullets: Garbage in, garbage out: if the coding agent's Blender program models the physics wrong, the 'verified' proxy just locks in the wrong answer with more confidence
Two extra heavyweight steps (code generation + simulation execution) run before the generative video engine even starts — meaningfully higher latency and compute than a single-pass T2V model
The public toy dataset is 8 hand-checked cases — illustrative of specific phenomena, not evidence the approach scales cleanly to arbitrary, open-ended scenes
Photorealistic restyling can still introduce texture-level inconsistencies (lighting, material appearance) that the geometry-locked proxy never had to solve

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Executable code as chain-of-thought is a stronger guarantee than sketches or keyframes because you can actually run it and check its output
Separating 'get the motion right' (simulation) from 'get the pixels right' (generative restyle) lets each engine specialize instead of one model doing both badly
The causality-verification step — a caused state can't appear before its cause — is a cheap, general check that's easy to reuse in other agentic video pipelines
Biggest open question: does this generalize past hand-checked toy phenomena to the long tail of real-world scenes?

questions.prompt: What makes VideoCoCo's chain-of-thought different from earlier sketch- or keyframe-based CoT for video generation?
options: It uses a larger language model to write longer captions
It's executable code (Blender simulation) that can actually be run and verified, not a static intermediate representation
It skips reasoning entirely and generates video in one pass
It only works on 2D animations, not 3D scenes
questions.explanation: Sketches and keyframes are non-executable or temporally sparse — they still leave physics to be interpolated. Executable simulation code fully specifies the temporal evolution and can be run and checked before any pixels are generated.

questions.prompt: Why does the first-stage 'clay proxy' video deliberately have no color or texture?
options: To save GPU memory during training
Because Blender can't render color
To isolate and verify motion, deformation, and causality before style is layered on, so physics errors don't hide behind photorealistic texture
Because the dataset only contains grayscale footage
questions.explanation: Stripping color/texture forces the verification step to judge motion and causality purely on shape and deformation — exactly the signals that a photorealistic render could otherwise mask.

questions.prompt: On PhyGenBench, VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558. What's the main caveat on that result?
options: The improvement is entirely due to a bigger base video model
It's only validated on a small, hand-checked set of toy physical phenomena, not broad open-domain scenes
PhyGenBench doesn't measure physical consistency
The comparison excludes all open-source baselines
questions.explanation: The public dataset released alongside VideoCoCo is 8 hand-checked video-to-video cases covering specific phenomena (buoyancy, melting, etc.) — illustrative, not a large-scale generalization test.

references.title: VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System (arXiv:2607.27380)

posts.title: Muse Spark 1.1: Meta's First Paid Model, Built for Agents
posts.subtitle: Meta finally opens a public API — and tunes the model for tool orchestration, not chat
posts.summary: On July 9, 2026, Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped Muse Spark 1.1 with a public, paid developer API — Meta's first — priced between GPT-5 mini and Claude Sonnet 4.6. It's tuned specifically for agentic orchestration: planning across external tools, zero-shot generalizing to new ones, and delegating to parallel subagents, and it tops rivals on tool-use benchmarks even where it trails on raw coding depth.

slides.title: Meta's first model you can actually pay to use
slides.body: Muse Spark 1.1 is Meta Superintelligence Labs' successor to the original Muse Spark ('Avocado', April 2026), which shipped only to a closed partner program. This one comes with a public 'Meta Model API' — priced access, open to developers.

slides.title: Meta needed a credible agentic story, not another chat model
slides.body: After a rocky Llama 4 cycle, Meta's frontier push has been about agentic capability specifically — tools, orchestration, multi-step planning — rather than competing head-on with GPT and Claude on raw benchmark leaderboards.
bullets: Mark Zuckerberg posted about it on X directly — his first post there in three years — signaling this launch mattered strategically, not just technically
The prior Muse Spark was partner-only; without a public API, Meta had no way to prove agentic claims to the broader developer market
Rivals (OpenAI, Anthropic) already had mature agent/tool-use ecosystems around GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8

slides.title: A multimodal reasoning model tuned for orchestration
slides.body: Muse Spark 1.1 is built for personal and developer agentic tasks that require planning and coordination across a range of external apps and services — not just answering questions well.
bullets: Trained to orchestrate multi-agent systems: it delegates subtasks to parallel subagents to finish projects faster than its predecessor
Zero-shot generalizes to new tools and services it wasn't explicitly trained on
Major reported gains specifically in tool/computer use, coding, and multimodal understanding over the earlier partner-only version

slides.title: Leads on tool use, trails on deep single-shot coding
slides.body: The pattern is consistent across Meta's own evaluation report and independent write-ups: Muse Spark 1.1 clearly leads on orchestration-heavy tool-use benchmarks like MCP Atlas, but Claude Opus 4.8 still leads on deep, single-agent coding tasks like SWE-Bench Pro.

slides.title: Where the orchestration focus shows up in practice
slides.body: Picture an agent asked to plan a multi-city trip: book flights, check a shared calendar, and stay under budget.
bullets: A model tuned only for single-turn coding would need the whole plan handed to it as one prompt
Muse Spark 1.1 is designed to split this into parallel subagents — one per app/service — and coordinate their outputs into one final plan
The 'zero-shot generalizes to new tools' claim matters here: it doesn't need every travel API pre-baked into training to use one it's never seen

slides.title: Pricing, availability, and where it doesn't win
slides.body: $1.25 per million input tokens / $4.25 per million output tokens — above OpenAI's entry-level GPT-5 mini and Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5, but below Claude Sonnet 4.6.
bullets: Public preview is US-only for now, not a global GA release
On raw agentic coding depth (SWE-Bench Pro: 61.5 vs. Opus 4.8's 69.2), it's not the model to reach for on hard, single-agent coding tasks
Choose by workload: tool-orchestration-heavy agents favor Muse Spark 1.1; deep autonomous coding still favors Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.5

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Meta's first public paid model API is a strategic agentic bet, not a generalist chat-model launch
It wins clearly on scaled tool-use/orchestration benchmarks (MCP Atlas) while trailing on deep single-agent coding (SWE-Bench Pro)
Mid-tier pricing ($1.25/$4.25 per M tokens) positions it between budget and premium frontier models
US-only public preview — treat availability and pricing as still evolving

questions.prompt: What is new about Muse Spark 1.1 compared to the original Muse Spark from April 2026?
options: It's Meta's first model with a public, paid developer API
It's Meta's first multimodal model
It's open-weight while the original was closed
It removed agentic capabilities to focus on chat
questions.explanation: The original Muse Spark ('Avocado') shipped only to a closed partner program. Muse Spark 1.1 is the first version with a public 'Meta Model API' that any developer can pay to access.

questions.prompt: On which benchmark does Muse Spark 1.1 most clearly outperform both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8?
options: SWE-Bench Pro
Terminal-Bench 2.1
MCP Atlas, a scaled tool-use benchmark
Meta's internal coding benchmark
questions.explanation: Muse Spark 1.1 scores 88.1 on MCP Atlas versus 82.2 (Opus 4.8) and 75.3 (GPT-5.5) — its clearest win, and consistent with its design focus on tool orchestration.

questions.prompt: Where does Muse Spark 1.1 trail the field most, and what does that suggest about picking a model for a task?
options: It trails on SWE-Bench Pro (deep single-agent coding) — pick it for tool-orchestration-heavy agents, not for hard autonomous coding
It trails on every benchmark, so it should be avoided entirely
It trails only on price, not on any benchmark
It trails on multimodal tasks, so use it for text-only workloads
questions.explanation: Opus 4.8 leads SWE-Bench Pro 69.2 to Muse Spark 1.1's 61.5. The benchmark spread argues for matching the model to the workload rather than picking one 'best overall' model.

posts.title: Multi-Head Latent Attention: Shrinking the KV Cache
posts.subtitle: Instead of sharing heads like GQA, compress what every head stores in the first place
posts.summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2, compresses each token's key and value into one small shared latent vector instead of reducing how many heads store separate K/V (GQA's approach). DeepSeek-V2's ablations show it cuts KV cache to roughly 4-14% of an MHA-equivalent while matching or beating MHA's modeling quality, at the cost of a more complex 'decoupled RoPE' path and a trickier implementation.

slides.title: The KV cache, not the weights, is the real memory bottleneck
slides.body: At long context, the memory a model needs to serve a request is dominated by its per-token key/value cache — not by the model's parameters. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), from DeepSeek-V2, attacks that cache directly.

slides.title: GQA reduces heads, but each head still caches full-resolution K/V
slides.body: Grouped-Query Attention already cuts cache size by sharing one K/V pair across a group of query heads — but every cached K and V vector is still a real, full-resolution vector.
bullets: More concurrent long-context requests means more KV cache resident in GPU memory at once — cache size directly caps how many requests you can batch
GQA's fix is architectural sharing (fewer distinct K/V pairs); it doesn't touch how much each stored vector costs
DeepSeek-V2's own ablations found GQA actually modeled worse than full MHA — the head-sharing trade cost some quality to save memory

slides.title: Compress what gets stored, not how many copies
slides.body: MLA takes a different axis entirely: project each token's key and value down into one small shared latent vector via a low-rank down-projection matrix, and cache only that latent — not per-head K/V.
bullets: At attention time, the latent is up-projected back into per-head keys and values using learned up-projection matrices
Those up-projections can be algebraically absorbed into the query and output projection matrices at inference — so the full-size K/V is never actually materialized in memory
Because the latent is shared and small, the cached footprint per token drops by roughly an order of magnitude versus MHA

slides.title: The catch: compression breaks rotary position embeddings
slides.body: RoPE rotates queries and keys based on position — but that rotation doesn't commute cleanly with MLA's down/up-projection. DeepSeek-V2's fix is 'decoupled RoPE.'
bullets: Queries and keys are split into two parts: a compressed 'content' part (no positional rotation, fully benefits from compression) and a small separate low-dimension 'RoPE' part that carries position info uncompressed
Only the small RoPE part bypasses compression — the bulk of the cache is still the compressed latent
This split is what makes MLA compatible with standard rotary embeddings at all, at the cost of extra implementation complexity over GQA's single, simpler path

slides.title: Smaller cache, and better quality than MHA — not just a trade

rows: What each K/V vector costs to store
~4-14% of MHA (DeepSeek-V2 ablations, small vs. large MoE)

slides.body: The DeepSeek-V2 team reports MLA held up better than MHA in their ablations, even outperforming it when tuned carefully — unlike GQA, which traded some quality away for its memory savings.

slides.title: Worked example: serving many long-context requests at once
slides.body: Picture a 128K-context request queue on a fixed GPU memory budget.
bullets: Under MHA-style caching, each long request reserves a full-resolution K/V cache per layer per head — only a handful of such requests fit before memory is exhausted
Under MLA, each request's cache is the same small shared latent per token — an order of magnitude smaller — so the same GPU memory now fits far more concurrent long-context requests

This is exactly why MLA became central to how DeepSeek-V2 and its successors could offer long context cheaply: the bottleneck it targets is the one that actually caps concurrency in production serving

slides.title: When MLA isn't the obvious choice
slides.body: The savings are real, but they come with real costs elsewhere.
bullets: Significantly more complex to implement than GQA — two separate query/key paths (compressed content + decoupled RoPE) instead of one
The matrix-absorption trick that avoids materializing full K/V only cleanly applies to the content score; the small decoupled-RoPE dimensions still add some cache back
It's proven inside the DeepSeek model family at scale — teams building from scratch on a tight timeline may find GQA's simplicity a better fit despite the quality trade-off
Retrofitting MLA onto an existing MHA/GQA checkpoint isn't a drop-in swap — it changes the attention computation graph, not just a config flag

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: GQA and MLA attack the KV cache from different axes: GQA shares vectors across heads, MLA compresses what each vector costs to store
MLA's decoupled RoPE trick is the key enabling piece — without it, compression and rotary embeddings are incompatible
In DeepSeek-V2's ablations, MLA didn't just save memory — it matched or beat MHA's modeling quality, unlike GQA's small quality trade-off
The real payoff shows up in production: smaller per-token cache means more concurrent long-context requests on the same hardware

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between how GQA and MLA reduce KV cache size?
options: GQA and MLA use the exact same mechanism
GQA shares K/V pairs across groups of query heads; MLA compresses each token's K/V into one small shared latent vector
GQA compresses vectors; MLA shares them across heads
MLA removes the KV cache entirely
questions.explanation: GQA reduces how many distinct K/V pairs exist by sharing across head groups, while still storing full-resolution vectors. MLA instead shrinks what each stored vector costs by projecting it into a compressed latent.

questions.prompt: Why does MLA need a 'decoupled RoPE' path instead of applying rotary embeddings directly to the compressed latent?
options: RoPE only works on 32-bit floats
Rotary rotation doesn't commute with the down/up-projection used to compress and reconstruct K/V, so a separate uncompressed positional path is needed
Decoupled RoPE is faster to compute, unrelated to compression
MLA doesn't actually use RoPE at all
questions.explanation: Applying rotation before compression and reconstructing after don't produce the same result as rotating the reconstructed vector directly — so DeepSeek-V2 splits off a small uncompressed dimension just to carry position.

questions.prompt: According to DeepSeek-V2's ablations, how does MLA's modeling quality compare to standard MHA, and how does that contrast with GQA?
options: MLA is worse than MHA, same as GQA
MLA matches or exceeds MHA quality, while GQA was slightly worse than MHA in the same ablations
Both MLA and GQA exceed MHA equally
Quality wasn't measured, only cache size
questions.explanation: This is what makes MLA notable beyond just memory savings: DeepSeek-V2 reports MLA matching or beating MHA's quality, whereas GQA traded away some quality for its cache reduction.

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tune a 175B Model by Training 0.02% of It
posts.subtitle: Freeze the pretrained weights, learn a low-rank update instead — and merge it back with zero added latency
posts.summary: LoRA freezes a pretrained model's weights entirely and learns a tiny low-rank update (two small matrices, B and A) injected into the attention projections. Because the update collapses to the same shape as the original weight matrix, it can be merged in after training for zero inference overhead — which is why almost every fine-tuning stack (and every multi-tenant model host) defaults to it today.

slides.title: One low-rank trick cut fine-tuning cost by orders of magnitude
slides.body: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), introduced by Hu et al. at Microsoft in 2021, doesn't touch a single one of a pretrained model's original weights. It learns a small correction instead — and that one design choice is why task-specific fine-tuning went from 'needs a GPU cluster' to 'fits on a single consumer card.'

slides.title: Full fine-tuning means a full-size checkpoint for every task
slides.body: Fine-tuning updates every parameter in the model, so the gradients and optimizer state you need during training are as large as the model itself — and the checkpoint you save afterward is a complete second copy.
bullets: A 175B-parameter model in fp16 is already ~350GB; Adam's optimizer state (momentum + variance) roughly triples the memory needed to train it
Ship 10 fine-tuned variants (one per customer or task) and you're storing and swapping 10 full-size checkpoints
Every one of those checkpoints also needs its own copy loaded to serve — expensive for anyone hosting more than a handful of variants

slides.title: Freeze W, learn ΔW as the product of two small matrices
slides.body: LoRA keeps the pretrained weight matrix W completely frozen. Next to it, it adds a trainable update ΔW = B·A, where A is a small r×k matrix and B is d×r — with rank r chosen far smaller than d or k (often 4, 8, or 16).
bullets: Only A and B are trained; W never receives a gradient update
A is initialized with small random values, B is initialized to all zeros — so at step 0, ΔW = 0 and the model starts exactly at its pretrained behavior
In practice it's applied to the attention projections (Wq and Wv are the common minimal choice; some setups extend it to Wk and Wo too)
An α/r scaling factor controls how strongly the learned update perturbs the frozen weights

slides.title: Why low rank works: fine-tuning updates live in a small subspace
slides.body: This isn't a compression trick applied after the fact — it's a bet, borne out empirically, that the *useful* update for adapting a pretrained model to a new task has low intrinsic rank, even though the full weight matrix does not.
bullets: Because B is zero-initialized, training starts as a no-op and gradually grows a small, structured correction
After training, B·A can be added directly into W (W' = W + B·A) — the merged matrix has the exact same shape as the original
That merge step is why LoRA adds zero inference latency, unlike adapter layers that insert extra sequential computation into the forward pass

slides.title: LoRA vs. the alternatives it replaced
bullets: Hu et al. report that for GPT-3 175B, LoRA cuts trainable parameters by roughly 10,000x and peak GPU memory during training by roughly 3x versus full fine-tuning with Adam

slides.title: Worked example: LoRA on a 7B model's attention weights
slides.body: Take a 7B-parameter model with hidden size 4,096 across 32 layers, applying LoRA with rank r=8 to just Wq and Wv in every layer.
bullets: Each frozen Wq or Wv is 4,096 × 4,096 = ~16.8M parameters — full fine-tuning of just those two matrices across 32 layers would train ~1.07B parameters
LoRA's A and B per matrix: (r × 4,096) + (4,096 × r) = 2 × 8 × 4,096 = 65,536 trainable parameters
Across both matrices and all 32 layers: 65,536 × 2 × 32 ≈ 4.2M trainable parameters — about 250x fewer than fine-tuning Wq/Wv alone, and a small fraction of a percent of the full 7B model
That's a checkpoint measured in tens of megabytes instead of gigabytes, which is what makes swapping dozens of task-specific adapters at serve time practical

slides.title: Where LoRA breaks down, and its natural extension
slides.body: Rank r is a real capacity limit, not a free lunch, and the base model still has to fit in memory during training.
bullets: Set r too low and the model can underfit tasks that require a large behavioral shift from the pretrained distribution (e.g. a totally new domain or language)
LoRA shrinks the *trainable* footprint, but the frozen base weights still have to be loaded in full precision (or close to it) for the forward/backward pass

QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) fixes that second limit by quantizing the frozen base model to 4-bit while keeping LoRA's adapters in higher precision — enabling fine-tuning of 65B-class models on a single 48GB GPU

Serving many merged variants still means picking one merge per request; multi-tenant servers instead keep adapters unmerged and swap B·A per request to serve hundreds of task variants from one loaded base model

slides.title: The core idea in three moves
bullets: Freeze the pretrained weights entirely — never update them
Learn a low-rank update B·A instead, sized by a rank r that's a tiny fraction of the original matrix dimensions
Merge B·A back into W after training for zero added inference cost, or keep it unmerged to swap task adapters on the fly

questions.prompt: During LoRA fine-tuning, what happens to the original pretrained weight matrix W?
options: It is frozen and never updated
It is quantized to 4-bit before training starts
It is replaced entirely by B·A
It is fine-tuned alongside A and B
questions.explanation: LoRA's entire memory and compute savings come from never touching W. Only the small matrices A and B receive gradients — W stays exactly as it was pretrained.

questions.prompt: Why does merging LoRA's update into W add zero latency at inference time?
options: Because B·A is computed on a separate GPU
Because B·A has the same shape as W, so W' = W + B·A is a single matrix indistinguishable from a normal weight
Because rank r is always equal to 1
Because the base model is quantized after merging
questions.explanation: B (d×r) times A (r×k) produces a d×k matrix — exactly W's shape. Adding it once after training gives a normal, single weight matrix, so serving looks identical to serving the unmodified base model.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of choosing LoRA's rank r too small for a given task?
options: Training runs slower than full fine-tuning
The optimizer state size doubles
The model can underfit tasks that need a large behavioral shift from the pretrained distribution
Inference latency increases proportionally to 1/r
questions.explanation: Rank r caps how much the update can express. A very small r is fine for narrow style/format adaptation but can be too limited for tasks that require the model to shift substantially from what it learned during pretraining.

references.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (Hu et al., 2021)

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: The Middle Ground That Made 70B Models Servable
posts.subtitle: Why Llama 2's 70B model shares 8 key-value heads across 64 query heads instead of one or sixty-four
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) splits query heads into small groups that each share one key-value head, landing between full multi-head attention (best quality) and multi-query attention (fastest, cheapest). Llama 2 70B uses it to cut KV-cache size 8x with almost no quality loss, which is why models past ~30B params ship with GQA by default today.

slides.title: One idea let 70B-parameter models fit a KV cache in memory
slides.body: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) is the attention variant that made large open models actually servable at long context. It's not a training trick — it's a change to how key/value heads are shared during inference.

slides.title: Multi-head attention makes the KV cache grow with every head you add
slides.body: During autoregressive decoding, a transformer caches every past token's key and value vectors per layer, per head, so it doesn't recompute them each step. With standard multi-head attention (MHA), each of the N query heads keeps its own K/V head — so the cache scales linearly with head count.
bullets: For a 70B model with 64 heads and 80 layers, a full MHA cache needs ~2.5 MB per token, per sequence
At 4,096 tokens of context, that's ~10 GB of GPU memory just for cache — before weights or activations
More heads means better quality, but every extra head is more memory bandwidth to move per decoding step

slides.title: Multi-query attention fixed memory but broke quality
slides.body: Google's 2019 fix, Multi-Query Attention (MQA), collapsed all K/V heads down to just one shared head — every query head reads the same keys and values. It slashes the cache but forces every head to attend the same way, which measurably hurts output quality on larger models.
bullets: MQA cache size: independent of head count — just 1 K/V pair per layer
Speed win is real: decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, so a smaller cache means faster token generation
Quality loss shows up on harder tasks (long-form reasoning, code) where per-head specialization matters

slides.title: GQA: split heads into G groups, each group shares one K/V head
slides.body: Ainslie et al. (Google Research, 2023, arXiv:2305.13245) proposed Grouped-Query Attention as a tunable middle point. Instead of 1 shared head (MQA) or N independent heads (MHA), you pick G groups: G=1 recovers MQA, G=N recovers MHA, and everything in between trades cache size for quality.
bullets: Existing MHA checkpoints can be 'uptrained' into GQA using ~5% of the original pretraining compute — no training from scratch
Llama 2 34B and 70B use GQA with G=8: 64 query heads grouped into 8, each group sharing 1 K/V head
Llama 2 7B and 13B kept plain MHA — GQA's benefit only matters once the KV cache itself becomes the bottleneck

slides.title: Same architecture, three attention variants, very different caches
bullets: Mistral 7B uses G=8 as well (32 query heads / 8 KV heads = groups of 4), pairing GQA with a 4,096-token sliding window for extra memory savings

slides.title: Worked example: the 8x cache drop, in actual gigabytes
slides.body: Llama 2 70B: 80 layers, hidden size 8192, 64 heads → head_dim = 128. KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) x kv_heads x head_dim x layers x 2 bytes (fp16).
bullets: MHA (64 KV heads): 2 x 64 x 128 x 80 x 2 bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token → ~10.2 GB at a 4,096-token context
GQA (8 KV heads): 2 x 8 x 128 x 80 x 2 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB/token → ~1.25 GB at the same 4,096 tokens
That's the difference between a cache that fits alongside the model weights on one GPU and one that doesn't

slides.title: Where GQA doesn't help — and what it costs you
slides.body: GQA is not free and not always the right call.
bullets: Small models rarely need it: below ~13B params, the KV cache usually isn't the memory bottleneck, so plain MHA's quality edge wins
The group count G is fixed at training/uptraining time — you can't change it per-request the way you'd change a batch size
Uptraining still costs real compute (~5% of pretraining) and a quality re-validation pass; it's not a free post-hoc toggle
GQA only reduces the KV cache — it does nothing for the O(n²) cost of computing attention scores itself (that's FlashAttention's job)

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: MHA = best quality, biggest cache. MQA = smallest cache, biggest quality risk. GQA = a tunable point between them
GQA groups N query heads into G groups, each sharing one K/V head; G=8 is a common sweet spot at 30B+ scale
Existing MHA checkpoints can be uptrained into GQA cheaply — you don't need to pretrain from scratch
Llama 2 34B/70B and Mistral 7B both ship GQA; smaller models (Llama 2 7B/13B) don't need it
GQA shrinks the KV cache, not attention's compute cost — pair it with FlashAttention/PagedAttention for the full picture

questions.prompt: In Llama 2 70B, 64 query heads are grouped into 8 groups. How many key-value heads does the model actually store?
questions.explanation: GQA gives each of the 8 groups its own shared K/V head, so there are 8 K/V heads total — the 64 query heads split evenly into those 8 groups, 8 query heads per K/V head.

questions.prompt: What happens if you set GQA's group count G equal to the total number of attention heads N?
options: You get Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
You recover standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA)
The model fails to run
The KV cache disappears entirely
questions.explanation: G=N means every query head gets its own dedicated K/V head — no sharing at all — which is exactly the definition of standard multi-head attention. G=1 is the other extreme, which is MQA.

questions.prompt: Why did Llama 2's 7B and 13B models skip GQA while the 34B and 70B models use it?
options: GQA only works on models with an even number of layers
Smaller models don't have a KV cache
At smaller scale, the KV cache isn't the memory bottleneck, so plain MHA's quality edge is worth keeping
GQA requires more training data than smaller models were given
questions.explanation: GQA's whole benefit is shrinking the KV cache, which only becomes a serving bottleneck at larger head counts and longer contexts. Below ~13B, that cache is small enough that it's not worth trading away MHA's quality.

references.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (Ainslie et al., 2023)

posts.title: SpyRL: A Spy Game Makes Open-Ended Tasks Verifiable
posts.subtitle: Reinforcement learning needs a right answer — this paper invents one by making agents vote out an impostor.
posts.summary: A team from Duke, Adobe, Oregon State, Penn State, NUS, and Amazon (arXiv:2607.23802) proposes RLSVR: transforming open-ended tasks like summarization and creative writing into a social-deduction game called SpyRL, where the reward comes from a rule-based vote outcome instead of a subjective judge. It reportedly beats existing self-improvement methods on non-verifiable tasks and still helps on already-verifiable math reasoning.

slides.title: When There's No Right Answer, RL Has Nothing to Reward
slides.body: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) made reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 possible — but it only works when you can automatically check the answer. Summarization and creative writing have no answer key. This paper invents one.

slides.title: RLVR's Whole Trick Is Also Its Ceiling
bullets: RLVR needs an automatic checker: a unit test for code, an answer key for math, a compiler for a proof — something that scores an output without a human in the loop
Creative writing, summarization, and open dialogue have no such checker; quality is inherently subjective
The usual workaround, a learned reward model, can be gamed as the policy shifts — the model learns to satisfy the scorer rather than to actually write better
Without a reliable reward, letting a model train on its own outputs (self-improvement) stalls out precisely on the tasks that most need it

slides.title: Turn the Task Into a Game With a Built-In Answer Key
bullets: RLSVR (Reinforcement Learning with Self-Verifiable Rewards) borrows a trick from self-supervised learning: transform a task into a proxy problem that has automatic, rule-based ground truth
Its instantiation, SpyRL, is a multi-agent social-deduction game modeled on 'Who Is the Spy?'
Several agent copies all attempt the same underlying task, but one secretly-chosen 'spy' is given different or degraded information to work from
The other agents vote on who the spy is by comparing outputs — the vote outcome, not a learned scorer, is the reward, so it's verifiable by construction

slides.title: Worked Example: Summarizing an Article, With One Impostor
slides.body: Picture four agents given the same article to summarize, plus a fifth 'spy' agent quietly handed a corrupted or partial version of it.
bullets: All five produce summaries; every agent then reads the full set and votes for whichever one looks like the odd one out
If the spy's missing information leaks through as a noticeably worse or inconsistent summary, the voters catch it — a correct vote is the reward signal

This creates pressure in both directions: the spy is pushed to produce quality good enough to blend in despite worse inputs, and voters are pushed to read carefully enough to notice when something's off
No human grades a single summary — the only thing ever checked is a discrete, rule-based outcome: was the spy correctly identified

slides.title: Three Ways to Get a Training Reward

rows: Automatic checker: unit test, answer key, compiler
No — only where a checker exists
A model trained on human preference labels
Yes, but driftable and gameable as the policy shifts
Rule-based outcome of a voting game
Yes — verifiable by construction, no learned judge

slides.title: What the Paper Reports
bullets: Across summarization and creative writing, SpyRL is reported to consistently outperform existing self-improvement baselines that rely on a learned reward model
It also yields further gains on tasks that already had a verifiable checker, like mathematical reasoning — the game-based signal adds something a plain answer-key reward didn't capture alone
The authors frame this as evidence that 'task transformation' — reshaping the problem so a rule can score it — is a more general lever than inventing new RL math
Exact benchmark scores weren't independently reconfirmed here; treat the direction (consistent gains) as the reliable claim, not any specific number

slides.title: Where This Trick Runs Into Limits
bullets: It only works when a task can plausibly be turned into an asymmetric-information game — not every task decomposes that way
The reward is a proxy: 'was the spy correctly identified,' not 'was the output actually good.' If voting agents are weak or biased, the signal gets noisy regardless of true quality
Running the game costs more compute per training step than a single reward-model call — you need N agent copies to produce outputs and then vote, every round
Because the reward is indirect, it's possible in principle for vote accuracy and human-judged quality to diverge, especially at the edges of what the voters can reliably detect

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RLVR's real limitation was never the algorithm — it was needing a checker at all, which excludes writing, summarization, and dialogue
SpyRL sidesteps this by making the reward the outcome of a game's rules (a vote), not a subjective or learned judge
The core idea — transform the task, don't reinvent the RL math — is what generalizes, echoing how self-supervised learning turned unlabeled data into pretext tasks with automatic labels
It reportedly helps even on already-verifiable math tasks, suggesting the 'catch the impostor' pressure is a general quality signal, not just a workaround

questions.prompt: What is the core problem RLVR faces on tasks like creative writing or summarization?
options: The tasks are too easy for current models
There's no automatic checker to verify if an output is "correct," since quality is subjective
The model's context window is too short for these tasks
RL training is too slow to ever be used for text generation
questions.explanation: RLVR's strength — a verifiable checker like a unit test or an answer key — is also its limit. It simply has no way to score a task with no ground truth.

questions.prompt: In SpyRL, how does the game actually generate a training reward?
options: A human rater manually scores each generated output
A separately trained reward model predicts a quality score
Agents vote on which participant received different or degraded information, and the vote's correctness produces the reward
The reward is based purely on how long the generated text is
questions.explanation: The reward is a rule-based function of the vote outcome — who gets correctly identified as the spy — not a subjective or learned judgment, so it's verifiable by construction just like checking a math answer.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what's a genuine limitation of an approach like SpyRL?
options: It only works on programming tasks
The reward is an indirect proxy (vote accuracy, not quality itself), and it needs multiple agent copies plus reliably capable voters each round
It cannot produce any gains on already-verifiable tasks
It completely removes the need for reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Vote accuracy is a proxy for quality, not quality itself, and running several agent copies and dependable voters per round adds real compute and reliability requirements.

references.title: From RLVR to RLSVR: Task Transformation Induces Self-Verifiable Rewards for Open-Ended LLM Self-Improvement (arXiv:2607.23802)

posts.title: Hermes Agent v0.20.0: Nous Ships A2A and Live Voice
posts.subtitle: 3,650 commits later, the open-source agent framework learns to talk to other agents and lets you interrupt it mid-sentence.
posts.summary: Nous Research shipped Hermes Agent v0.20.0 on August 3, 2026 — a 3,650-commit, 1,400-PR release for the 225k-star open-source agent framework. Highlights: an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) v1.0 protocol plugin for cross-vendor agent interoperability, streaming voice with true barge-in, grounded-citation research, and cold start cut from ~14s to ~1.8s.

slides.title: An Open-Source Agent Just Learned to Talk to Other Agents
slides.body: Hermes Agent, Nous Research's self-hosted AI agent framework (225k+ GitHub stars), shipped v0.20.0 on August 3, 2026 — its biggest release yet, closing one of the repo's oldest feature requests.

slides.title: What Was Missing Before v0.20.0
bullets: Hermes Agent runs as a self-improving agent across CLI, desktop, and chat platforms (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal), with persistent memory and autonomous skill creation
Issue #514 — a request for Hermes to discover and interoperate with agents from other frameworks — had sat open as one of the oldest feature requests in the repo
Voice interaction existed, but without true 'barge-in': you couldn't interrupt the agent mid-response the way you can with a person
Cold start took roughly 14 seconds, real friction for a tool meant to feel instant on the command line

slides.title: What v0.20.0 Actually Ships
bullets: An A2A Protocol v1.0 plugin: Hermes can now discover, talk to, and be driven by other A2A-compatible agents — directly closing issue #514
Streaming, conversational text-to-speech with barge-in across CLI, desktop, and gateway, plus on-device wake words that never send audio off the machine
A grounded-citations research skill: every claim is backed by a source, with quotes matched against actual page text instead of being hallucinated
Desktop gets sandboxed live-preview artifacts, a plugin SDK (with a Kanban board as the first plugin), global quick-entry, and SSH remote-backend support

slides.title: Worked Example: Handing a Task to a Different Vendor's Agent
slides.body: Say a Hermes agent needs to hand off part of a workflow to a completely different coding-agent product that also speaks A2A v1.0.
bullets: Hermes discovers the other agent through A2A's discovery mechanism — no custom, one-off integration code per vendor
It can hand off the subtask and receive results back, or let the other agent drive part of the workflow directly
This is the same idea as two different email clients being able to reach each other because they both speak SMTP — a shared wire protocol beats a pile of point-to-point integrations
Paired with the release's new outbound webhooks, downstream systems can react the instant a handoff completes, instead of polling for status

slides.title: Before vs. After v0.20.0
Where This Release Isn't a Fit
bullets: Self-hosting a 225k-star, 20,000+-commit codebase is a real operational commitment — you own security patching, plugin vetting, and infrastructure for a CLI, a desktop app, and multiple chat-platform bots
A2A interoperability only helps if the other agents you want to reach also implement A2A v1.0 — it doesn't retrofit compatibility with closed, non-A2A platforms
On-device wake words keep audio local, but that also means voice quality is bounded by whatever hardware you're running on, unlike a cloud-routed voice API
Teams that want a zero-maintenance, hosted agent may be better served by a managed product than by adopting a fast-moving framework that ships major versions every few months

slides.title: The Release, By the Numbers
bullets: ~3,650 commits and ~1,400 merged PRs since the previous version, touching roughly 5,200 files, from 647 contributors
That's the release cadence of a well-funded product team, not a research lab's side project — a sign of how much community investment self-hosted agent tooling is attracting
Combined with the framework's existing 225k+ GitHub stars, it's one of the largest open agent projects by contributor activity right now

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (Aug 3, 2026) adds an A2A v1.0 plugin, letting the open agent interoperate with other A2A-compatible agents for the first time
Streaming voice with real barge-in, source-grounded research citations, and a cold start cut from ~14s to ~1.8s round out the release
It's backed by real scale: roughly 3,650 commits and 1,400 PRs from 647 contributors in one cycle
The tradeoff of self-hosting real agent infrastructure is ongoing maintenance — weigh that against a managed alternative before adopting it

posts.title: RoPE: Baking Position Into Attention Through Rotation
posts.subtitle: No position embedding table to look up — just rotate each vector by an angle that depends on where it sits.
posts.summary: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) encode a token's position by rotating its query and key vectors by an angle proportional to that position, instead of adding a value from a lookup table. Because rotating two vectors before their dot product is equivalent to rotating by their position difference afterward, attention scores end up depending only on relative distance — which is exactly why RoPE-based models are the ones context-extension tricks like YaRN target.

slides.title: Position Doesn't Live in a Table — It Lives in an Angle
slides.body: Self-attention has no built-in sense of token order: shuffle the inputs and the raw dot products don't care. RoPE fixes this by rotating each query and key vector by an angle proportional to its position, so order falls directly out of the math attention already does.

slides.title: Attention Is Naturally Blind to Order
bullets: Self-attention computes weighted sums via dot products between tokens — shuffle the input sequence and those raw scores are unchanged, since nothing about the computation references position

The original Transformer added a fixed sinusoidal position vector to each token embedding at the input. It works, but that positional signal has to survive every subsequent layer of matrix multiplication to still matter

Learned absolute position embeddings (a trained lookup table per position, as in early GPT/BERT) hit a hard wall: there's no valid embedding for position 2049 if training only ever saw sequences up to length 2048
Neither approach directly encodes relative distance between two tokens — which is the thing attention actually uses to decide what's nearby and relevant

slides.title: Rotate the Query and Key Vectors by an Angle
bullets: RoPE (Su et al., RoFormer, 2021) splits each query/key vector into 2D pairs of dimensions and rotates each pair by an angle θ = position × frequency
Different dimension-pairs rotate at different frequencies: low-index pairs rotate fast and capture fine-grained local position, high-index pairs rotate slowly and capture coarse, long-range position
Rotating both the query at position m and the key at position n means their dot product ends up depending only on the angle difference — i.e., on (m − n), the relative position
There's no embedding table involved: the rotation is a deterministic function computed on the fly, so there's nothing that can 'run out' at long sequence lengths the way a lookup table can

slides.title: Worked Example: Why the Dot Product Only Sees the Gap
slides.body: A property of rotation matrices makes this work: rotating two vectors by angles mθ and nθ before taking their dot product gives the same result as taking the dot product first and then rotating by (m − n)θ.
bullets: Concretely: a query at position 5 attending to a key at position 8 produces the same relative angle as a query at position 100 attending to a key at position 103 — both are a gap of 3
This is why RoPE-based models can often extrapolate somewhat past their trained context length: the mechanism only ever 'sees' a relative distance, never an absolute index it wasn't trained on

It's also why context-extension techniques like YaRN and NTK-aware scaling work by rescaling RoPE's rotation frequencies rather than by inventing new position embeddings for positions the model never saw

slides.title: Three Ways to Encode Position

rows: Absolute position via a lookup table
No — undefined past the table's size
Absolute position via a fixed formula
Weakly — still injects an absolute bias
Relative position via a rotation angle
Better — relative signal, plus rescaling tricks like YaRN

slides.title: Where RoPE Still Has Limits
bullets: RoPE doesn't grant unlimited context on its own — quality still degrades well before any rotation math 'breaks,' since attention itself gets diluted across too many tokens regardless of how position is encoded
Rotation frequencies are normally fixed at pretraining time; running a RoPE model far past its trained length without a rescaling trick causes attention quality to degrade gradually, not fail cleanly
It adds a small amount of per-layer compute (the rotation itself) versus a plain embedding addition — cheap relative to attention, but not literally free

Nearly every major open-weight LLM (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek) uses RoPE today, which also means a subtle bug in how it's applied — like the wrong base frequency — silently degrades long-context behavior instead of crashing loudly

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RoPE encodes position by rotating query/key vectors, not by adding a value pulled from a lookup table
Because rotating both vectors before their dot product is equivalent to rotating by their position difference afterward, attention scores end up depending only on relative position
That relative-only property is exactly what makes context-extension tricks like YaRN and NTK-aware scaling possible — they rescale rotation frequencies instead of training new position embeddings
It's the default positional scheme in nearly every modern open-weight LLM, precisely because it generalizes better to long and variable-length sequences than the absolute schemes it replaced

questions.prompt: What does RoPE do to a query or key vector to encode its position?
options: Adds a learned vector pulled from a position lookup table
Concatenates a one-hot position vector onto it
Rotates pairs of its dimensions by an angle proportional to position
Multiplies the whole vector by the sequence length
questions.explanation: RoPE splits each vector into 2D pairs and rotates each pair by an angle equal to position × a frequency — an operation applied to the vector, not a lookup or an added constant.

questions.prompt: Why does RoPE end up encoding relative position instead of absolute position?
options: It doesn't — RoPE only ever encodes absolute position
Rotating the query at position m and the key at position n before their dot product is equivalent to rotating by (m − n) afterward, so the result depends only on the gap
Because positions are hashed before being rotated
Because only the key vector is rotated, never the query
questions.explanation: A rotation-matrix identity makes the effective angle in the dot product equal to the difference between the two rotation angles, so only the relative distance (m − n) survives into the attention score.

questions.prompt: Why do context-extension techniques like YaRN specifically target RoPE?
options: Because RoPE has no tunable parameters at all
Because RoPE's position signal comes from adjustable rotation frequencies, unlike a fixed-size lookup table that has nothing to rescale
Because RoPE requires full retraining before context length can change at all
Because RoPE is only used in vision models, where extension is easier
questions.explanation: Since RoPE's position signal comes from rotation frequencies rather than a fixed table of trained vectors, techniques like YaRN can rescale those frequencies to stretch effective context length without training new embeddings for positions the model never saw.

posts.title: Metis: A Model That Remembers Without Retrieving
posts.subtitle: Native memory lives inside the weights, updated with a single forward pass — no vector database, no gradient step.
posts.summary: MemTensor's Metis (arXiv:2607.26760, July 2026) gives a language model a native memory state inside its own computation, updated with a gradient-free forward pass instead of retrieval or fine-tuning. Built on Qwen3.5 at 4B/9B/27B scales, it beats prior memory baselines on long-horizon QA benchmarks — but the memory is fixed-size and opaque, unlike a RAG index you can inspect.

slides.title: Memory That Lives Inside the Weights
slides.body: Most AI 'memory' today means a vector database bolted onto a model: embed the past, retrieve the closest match, stuff it into the prompt. Metis tries something structurally different — a memory state that is part of the model's own forward pass.

slides.title: Bolt-On Memory Has a Ceiling
bullets: RAG-style agent memory retrieves external chunks by embedding similarity — the model itself never actually learns anything from a conversation
Every new memory means re-embedding and re-indexing outside the model, adding a whole separate storage system to maintain
Top-k retrieval is lossy by construction: whatever doesn't make the cut is invisible to the model, no matter how relevant
The model's weights stay frozen — memory is something it looks up, not something it has

slides.title: A Memory Block Inside the Forward Pass
bullets: Each Metis Block pairs a Local Memory Block (holds the persistent state) with a Hyper Memory Block (learns how to store and use it)
Inspired by Fast Weight Programming: the model's own activations write into a compact memory state, no external database involved
The default update rule is a Gated Delta Network — memory attention later reads that state and fuses it with ordinary attention
Large-scale memory-specific training data teaches these store/retrieve procedures during mid-training, before the model ever sees a real memory task

slides.title: Gradient-Free: The Update Is Just a Forward Pass
bullets: Writing a new memory does not touch the model's learned weights at all — no backward pass, no optimizer step, no fine-tuning run
At inference time, all weights stay frozen; only the memory state itself changes, produced by standard forward computation
That makes memory updates as cheap as a normal inference call — you can write to memory mid-conversation without stopping to retrain anything
Checkpoints ship at 4B, 9B, and 27B, all built on top of Qwen3.5 backbones

slides.title: Three Ways an LLM Can 'Remember'

rows: A memory state inside the forward pass

slides.title: Worked Example: Answering Without the Original Text
slides.body: On MemDaily, a benchmark testing recall of everyday conversational facts, Metis-27B was evaluated in a 'no-context' setting — the original conversation is gone, only the memory state remains.
bullets: Metis-27B averages 59.04 on MemDaily and 18.56 on ATM-Bench under this no-original-context condition
That score has to come entirely from what the memory state compressed earlier — there's no chunk of text to re-read
The paper reports this beats prior memory baselines like Temp-LoRA and δ-Mem, which rely on fine-tuning-style updates or external stores
This is the real test of whether the memory 'stuck' — not whether the model can still see the source

slides.title: Where Native Memory Still Breaks
bullets: The paper reports performance degrading rapidly once a single input stretches past a few hundred words — long documents are still a weak spot
Memory state size is fixed by architecture, unlike a vector store that can grow to millions of entries
There's no plaintext memory to inspect — you can't open the memory state and read what it 'remembers' the way you can read a retrieved RAG chunk
Acquiring this memory behavior requires mid-training on purpose-built data; you can't bolt native memory onto an arbitrary existing checkpoint

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Metis treats memory as part of the forward pass, not an external lookup — a structurally different bet from RAG-style agent memory
Updates are gradient-free: one forward pass writes to memory, no fine-tuning required
It beats prior memory baselines on no-original-context QA benchmarks (e.g., 59.04 avg on MemDaily) at 4B–27B scale
The tradeoff: a fixed-size, opaque memory state versus a growable, inspectable index — pick based on whether you need to audit what's stored

questions.explanation: The whole point is that a memory write costs the same as a normal inference call — the model's learned weights never move, only the compact memory state does.

Metis requires more external storage than RAG

options: It cannot run on GPUs

questions.explanation: Despite beating baselines on no-context recall, the paper reports the model's performance drops off quickly on longer individual inputs — native memory hasn't solved long-context robustness generally.

posts.title: Function Calling: How an LLM Actually Invokes a Tool
posts.subtitle: The model doesn't run code — it emits structured text that your runtime decides to execute.
posts.summary: Every agent framework 'calls tools,' but the model never executes anything — it predicts structured text that matches a schema, and your code decides whether to run it. Understanding the token-level mechanics explains why tool calls fail in specific, fixable ways.

slides.title: The Model Never Actually Calls Anything
slides.body: When people say an LLM 'calls a tool,' what happens under the hood is narrower: the model predicts tokens that match a name and a JSON payload. Your application reads that output and decides whether to run the real function.

slides.title: Free-Form Text Doesn't Reliably Become Valid JSON
bullets: Ask a model to 'reply with JSON' in plain prompting and you'll get trailing commentary, markdown fences, or almost-valid JSON often enough to break a parser in production
Nested schemas (an object inside an array inside an object) multiply the ways a free-form completion can go wrong
A single missing quote or comma fails the whole call — there's no partial credit for 'almost right' JSON
Retrying blind (just asking again) burns tokens and latency without fixing the underlying cause

slides.title: Three Layers That Make Tool Calls Reliable
bullets: Schema definition: each tool is described with a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for its parameters — this is what the model conditions on
Structured decoding: many APIs (OpenAI function calling, Anthropic tool use) constrain generation so the output is forced to match the schema's shape, not just prompted to
Runtime dispatch: your code reads the model's tool-call output, validates it again independently, then executes the real function and returns the result as a new message
The loop repeats: the tool result goes back into context, and the model decides whether to call another tool or respond to the user

slides.title: Constrained Decoding Is What Makes This Reliable
bullets: Under the hood, constrained decoding restricts which tokens are even eligible at each generation step, based on the schema's grammar — the model literally cannot emit a token that breaks JSON syntax
This is different from just prompting the model to output JSON: constrained decoding intervenes at the sampling step itself, not just the prompt
Libraries like Guidance and Outlines, plus hosted APIs' native JSON/tool modes, use this technique server-side
The model still picks which tool to call and what values to fill in — constraint only guarantees the shape is valid, not that the content is correct

slides.title: Worked Example: A Weather Agent
slides.body: User asks 'what should I wear in Boston tomorrow?' The model has one tool available: get_weather(location: string, date: string).
bullets: Turn 1: the model emits a tool call — get_weather({"location": "Boston, MA", "date": "2026-08-05"}) — instead of a direct answer
Your runtime validates the arguments, calls the real weather API, and gets back {"tempF": 68, "condition": "rain"}
That result is appended to the conversation as a tool message, and the model is called again with it in context
Turn 2: the model now writes a normal text reply — 'Bring a rain jacket, it'll be 68°F and rainy' — using the tool result it never saw until this turn

slides.title: Prompted JSON vs. Structured Tool Calls

rows: Extra prose, markdown fences, malformed syntax
Valid JSON, but wrong shape or missing fields
Valid JSON matching the exact schema
Wrong values or wrong tool choice — but never malformed

slides.title: Where Tool Calling Still Goes Wrong
bullets: Constrained decoding guarantees shape, not correctness — a model can still hallucinate a plausible-looking but wrong argument value
Deeply nested or highly overlapping tool schemas increase the chance the model picks the wrong tool, even with valid-JSON output
Long tool lists degrade selection accuracy — most providers recommend keeping active tools to a focused, task-relevant set rather than exposing dozens at once
Tool calling adds a full extra round trip (call, execute, re-call) — for latency-sensitive UIs, that's real added time even when everything works correctly

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The model never runs code — it predicts structured text; your runtime decides whether and how to execute it
Constrained decoding is what turns 'please output JSON' into a hard guarantee: it restricts which tokens are legal at each generation step
Even with a guaranteed-valid shape, the model can still pick the wrong tool or hallucinate wrong argument values — validate content, not just syntax
Keep the active tool list small and schemas flat where possible; both directly improve selection accuracy

questions.prompt: What does "constrained decoding" actually change about how a model generates a tool call?
options: It fine-tunes the model on more examples
It restricts which tokens are eligible at each generation step so the output can't break the schema's syntax
It runs the output through a separate JSON validator after generation, with no change to generation itself
It disables tool calling entirely
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding intervenes at the sampling step itself — the model is prevented from emitting a token that would produce invalid JSON, rather than just being asked nicely to format its output.

questions.prompt: A tool call comes back with syntactically perfect JSON, but the "location" field doesn't match what the user asked for. What does this show?
options: Constrained decoding failed
Schema validity and content correctness are separate guarantees — constrained decoding only ensures the former
The tool schema was malformed
This is impossible with structured output
questions.explanation: Structured decoding guarantees the shape of the output, not the truth of its content. A model can still hallucinate a wrong-but-valid argument value.

questions.prompt: Why do most providers recommend keeping the number of active tools small in a single request?
options: APIs charge extra per tool defined
A longer tool list degrades the model's accuracy at picking the right tool for the task
JSON Schema doesn't support more than 5 tools
It's a hard technical limit that always errors past 10 tools
questions.explanation: Even with valid-JSON guarantees, tool selection accuracy drops as the list of available tools grows — a focused, task-relevant tool set improves the odds the model picks correctly.

posts.title: Qwen-UI-Agent: A Foundation Model for Every Screen

posts.summary: Alibaba's Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report (July 2026) trains one GUI agent to operate phones, desktops, browsers, and a command line through a unified action space, using a self-generating data flywheel and large-scale online RL. It sets new mobile-use benchmarks and holds its own against frontier models on computer and browser use.

slides.title: One Agent Learns to Use Every Screen
slides.body: Most GUI agents specialize: one model for mobile taps, another for desktop clicks, another for browser DOM actions. Qwen-UI-Agent trains a single foundation model across all of them — plus a command line — using one unified way of describing an action.

slides.title: Why One Model Per Surface Doesn't Scale
bullets: Mobile, desktop, and browser agents are usually trained separately, so skills learned on one surface don't transfer to another
Most public GUI-agent training data caps out well under 20-turn trajectories — far short of real multi-app tasks that chain dozens of steps
Benchmarks built on a handful of curated apps don't capture real device diversity, so agents overfit to benchmark UIs
Treating GUI actions (taps, clicks) and CLI actions (shell commands) as separate action spaces forces an agent to pick a mode instead of freely mixing both

slides.title: A Unified Action Space Plus a Self-Generating Curriculum
bullets: One action space interleaves GUI operations (taps, swipes, clicks) with CLI execution, and can emit several batched actions in a single model turn
An AutoResearch-style data flywheel: agents construct their own tasks and environments, diagnose their own failures, and plan the next round of training data
Online RL trains directly on trajectories exceeding 100 turns — long enough to capture real multi-app workflows, not toy demos
Over 10,000 concurrent sandboxed environments run in parallel to keep rollout collection fast enough to feed that scale of RL

slides.title: State of the Art on Mobile, Competitive Everywhere Else

rows: 2nd overall, ahead of GPT-5.5 & Gemini 3.1 Pro

slides.title: Worked Example: A Task That Spans Three Surfaces
slides.body: Ask it to 'book the cheapest flight under $400 and add it to my budget spreadsheet.' A siloed agent needs a human to bridge steps between apps. Qwen-UI-Agent's unified action space lets one model check a price on a travel app (mobile), open a comparison site (browser), and run a shell command to append a row to a local CSV — chaining GUI and CLI actions inside the same trajectory.

bullets: OSWorld-v2, a harder computer-use benchmark, gets only 40.0% partial-progress credit — full multi-step desktop autonomy is still unsolved
The training recipe leans on 10,000+ concurrent environments and 100+ turn RL rollouts — infrastructure far beyond what most teams can replicate
State of the art on mobile doesn't mean state of the art everywhere: on OSWorld-Verified it ranks 2nd, not 1st
A model trained to batch multiple actions per turn also needs stronger safeguards — one bad turn now executes several actions instead of one

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Qwen-UI-Agent trains a single foundation model across mobile, desktop, browser, and CLI action spaces instead of one model per surface
Its data flywheel lets agents generate and diagnose their own training tasks, feeding 100+ turn online RL across 10,000+ parallel environments
It sets new state of the art on mobile-use benchmarks (82.1% MobileWorld, 97.5% AndroidDaily) and lands competitively — but not first — on desktop and browser use
Harder desktop benchmarks (OSWorld-v2, 40% partial credit) show general computer-use autonomy is still an open problem
