posts.title: GPT-5.6: OpenAI Ships Three Models Instead of One
posts.subtitle: Sol, Terra, and Luna split flagship reasoning from cheap speed — and the model can now write code to run its own tools.
posts.summary: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 went generally available on July 9, 2026 as three separately priced tiers — Sol, Terra, Luna — plus Programmatic Tool Calling, where the model writes short programs to chain tool calls instead of round-tripping to the API after every step. It leads agentic benchmarks like Terminal-Bench and OSWorld, but still trails Claude Fable 5 on repository-level coding.

slides.title: One flagship model can't price for every job
slides.body: On July 9, 2026, OpenAI took GPT-5.6 fully public as a three-tier family — Sol, Terra, and Luna — after a limited June 26 preview restricted to about 20 vetted organizations.

slides.title: A single price point forces every task to pay flagship rates
slides.body: A quick classification call and a six-hour autonomous coding run have wildly different cost and latency needs — but most model families ship one main SKU.
bullets: Cheap, high-volume tasks (routing, extraction, short chat turns) don't need frontier reasoning depth
Long, hard, autonomous tasks need it and can tolerate the extra cost and latency
Splitting a release into explicit tiers up front — rather than one model with a 'fast mode' toggle — makes the tradeoff visible to whoever's paying the bill

slides.title: Three tiers, three jobs
slides.body: Sol is the flagship for hard, long-horizon autonomous work. Terra is the balanced default, roughly matching the prior GPT-5.5. Luna is the fast, cheap tier for high-volume work.
bullets: Sol (fast mode): $12.5 / $75 per million input/output tokens
Terra: $2.5 / $15 per million input/output tokens
Luna: $1 / $6 per million input/output tokens
All three share a roughly 1.05M-token context window, with 128K max output tokens on the flagship

slides.title: Programmatic Tool Calling: the model writes the glue code
slides.body: Instead of calling one tool, waiting for the model to see the result, then calling the next tool, GPT-5.6 can write a short JavaScript program that chains several tool calls together.
bullets: The program runs inside a sandboxed V8 runtime with no network access — it only orchestrates already-approved tool calls
Intermediate results are processed in that runtime instead of being round-tripped back through the model each step
OpenAI cites 38%–63.5% token reductions on tool-heavy workflows for early customers who adopted it
It's Responses-API-only — Chat Completions integrations don't get this without a migration

slides.title: What that looks like in practice
slides.body: Say an agent needs to pull data from three APIs, join the results, and filter for anomalies.
bullets: Old pattern: call API 1 → return to model → call API 2 → return to model → call API 3 → return to model → ask model to join/filter → done. Five+ round trips.
Programmatic Tool Calling pattern: the model writes one small program that calls all three APIs, joins and filters the data in-runtime, and hands back only the final result — one round trip
The savings compound with the number of tool calls in the chain, which is why OpenAI's cited gains cluster around long, tool-heavy agent workflows rather than single-turn chat

slides.title: Strong on agentic benchmarks, not the top on raw coding
slides.body: GPT-5.6's edge is agentic: terminal use, multi-step tool coordination, long-horizon tasks. On repository-level code generation, Claude Fable 5 still leads.

slides.title: Read the SWE-Bench Pro gap with a grain of salt
slides.body: Sol's 64.6% sits well below Claude Fable 5's reported 80% on the same benchmark — but the benchmark itself is under scrutiny.
bullets: OpenAI published a separate analysis arguing roughly 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks are broken or mis-specified, and urged developers to examine results carefully rather than take the headline score at face value
Programmatic Tool Calling only pays off on genuinely tool-heavy, multi-step workflows — a single-tool-call task won't see the reported savings
Three separately priced tiers mean more decisions for developers up front: picking the wrong tier is a real cost/quality tradeoff, not just a knob

slides.title: What to take from this release
bullets: Tiered pricing (Sol/Terra/Luna) is OpenAI matching cost to task difficulty explicitly, instead of one model for everything
Programmatic Tool Calling is the more structurally interesting change — code-as-orchestration cuts the model-API round-trip tax for agents
Pick Sol for autonomous, long-horizon agent work; Terra for balanced everyday use; Luna for high-volume, latency-sensitive calls
For pure code generation quality, this release doesn't unseat Claude Fable 5 — GPT-5.6's strength is agentic tool orchestration

questions.prompt: What differentiates the three GPT-5.6 tiers?
options: They're identical models with different rate limits
Sol, Terra, and Luna trade off capability, speed, and price for different task profiles
Only Sol supports tool calling
They are region-locked variants of the same weights
questions.explanation: Sol targets hard, long-horizon autonomous work at the highest cost; Terra is the balanced default; Luna is the fast, cheap tier for high-volume tasks — same family, different cost/capability tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: What does Programmatic Tool Calling actually change?
options: It lets the model access the internet directly from its sandbox
It replaces tool calling with pure text generation
The model writes a short program that chains multiple tool calls and processes results in-runtime, instead of round-tripping to the model after each call
It's a UI feature for visually building tool call chains
questions.explanation: The model writes JavaScript executed in a sandboxed, network-isolated V8 runtime that orchestrates already-approved tool calls — cutting the token and latency cost of repeated model round-trips on multi-step tasks.

questions.prompt: Why should you be cautious reading GPT-5.6 Sol's 64.6% SWE-Bench Pro score against Claude Fable 5's 80%?
options: The two models were tested on different hardware
OpenAI itself flagged that roughly 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks may be broken or mis-specified
SWE-Bench Pro doesn't test coding at all
Claude Fable 5's score was never independently verified
questions.explanation: OpenAI published analysis arguing a meaningful fraction of SWE-Bench Pro's tasks are broken, and cautioned against over-indexing on the raw percentage — a useful reminder that even widely-cited benchmarks can have measurement noise.

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Giving Every Chunk Back Its Context
posts.subtitle: A chunk that doesn't know what document it came from can't be found by the query that needs it.
posts.summary: Standard RAG chunks a document and embeds each piece in isolation, so a chunk like 'revenue grew 3% from the prior quarter' loses which company or quarter it's about. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by prepending a short LLM-written summary to each chunk before indexing — cutting retrieval failures by up to 67% when combined with reranking, according to Anthropic's own benchmarks.

slides.title: A chunk that forgot its own context
slides.body: Split a document into pieces, embed each piece alone, and you've thrown away exactly the information a search query needs to find it again.

slides.title: Chunking strips the context that makes a chunk findable
slides.body: Traditional RAG splits a document into 100-200 token chunks and embeds each one on its own, independent of its neighbors.
bullets: A chunk reading 'The company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' says nothing about which company or which quarter once it's separated from the document
A query for 'ACME Corp Q2 2023 revenue growth' won't match that chunk well semantically — none of those specific terms are actually in it
The chunk isn't wrong or irrelevant — it's just been made unfindable by the act of chunking

slides.title: Prepend context before you embed or index
slides.body: For each chunk, an LLM reads the whole source document plus that chunk, and writes a short (50-100 token) note that situates it — then that note is prepended before embedding and BM25 indexing.
bullets: Example: 'This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME Corp's Q2 2023 performance; the prior quarter's revenue was $314 million.' gets glued onto the original chunk text
Two techniques are applied together: Contextual Embeddings (fixes semantic/vector search) and Contextual BM25 (fixes exact keyword/lexical search)
Prompt caching keeps this affordable: the whole document is cached once, so generating context for every chunk in it doesn't mean re-reading and re-paying for the full document each time

slides.title: Before and after, side by side
slides.body: The underlying text doesn't change — only what gets embedded and indexed does.
bullets: Before: "The company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter."
After: "This chunk is from ACME Corp's Q2 2023 SEC filing; the prior quarter's revenue was $314M. The company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter."
A query like 'What was ACME's Q2 2023 revenue growth?' now shares real terms and semantic content with the indexed chunk instead of relying on the original sentence alone

slides.title: The numbers, stacked
slides.body: Anthropic measured retrieval failure rate (top-20 chunks) on their internal benchmark as each technique was layered on.

slides.title: When it doesn't pay for itself
slides.body: Contextual Retrieval adds real cost and complexity — it's not free, and it doesn't fix every retrieval problem.
bullets: It costs one extra LLM call per chunk at indexing time; prompt caching makes this cheap but not zero, especially for huge or fast-changing corpora
Reranking adds latency at query time — fine for a chat assistant, potentially too slow for a hard real-time system
Short, already self-contained chunks (a FAQ entry, a single tweet) see little benefit — there's not much missing context to restore
None of this helps if the answer simply isn't in the corpus — Contextual Retrieval improves *finding* relevant chunks, not the completeness of your knowledge base

slides.title: The core idea to remember
bullets: Chunking for RAG destroys context by design — Contextual Retrieval restores just enough of it before indexing to make search work
Combine both a semantic fix (Contextual Embeddings) and a lexical fix (Contextual BM25) — they catch different kinds of misses
Layer reranking on top for the largest gain, if your latency budget allows it
Best fit: large document collections where chunks currently read as ambiguous or context-free out of place

questions.prompt: What core problem does Contextual Retrieval address?
options: Documents being too large to fit in a context window
Chunks losing the surrounding context that would make them matchable to a relevant query
Embedding models being too slow for production
BM25 being deprecated in favor of vector search
questions.explanation: Splitting a document into independent chunks strips out exactly the context (which document, which section, which entity) that a search query relies on to find the right chunk.

questions.prompt: Which two indexing techniques does Contextual Retrieval combine?
options: Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25
Fine-tuning and prompt engineering
Quantization and distillation
Reranking and chunking size tuning
questions.explanation: Contextual Embeddings improves semantic/vector matching and Contextual BM25 improves exact lexical matching — using both catches more of the ways a chunk could otherwise be missed.

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's benchmark, what happens to retrieval failure rate when Contextual Embeddings, Contextual BM25, and reranking are all combined?
options: It stays roughly the same as the baseline
It drops from 5.7% to 1.9%, a 67% relative reduction
It increases due to added complexity
It only improves for very short documents
questions.explanation: Each layer compounds: contextual embeddings alone cut the failure rate to 3.7%, adding contextual BM25 brings it to 2.9%, and adding reranking on top brings it to 1.9% — a 67% relative reduction from the 5.7% baseline.

posts.title: Reflexion: How an Agent Learns From Its Own Failures
posts.subtitle: No gradient updates — just a memory of what went wrong last time.
posts.summary: Reflexion turns a failed attempt into a written note-to-self: an evaluator flags the mistake, a reflection step describes it in plain language, and the next attempt reads that note before trying again. No weights change — the improvement lives entirely in an episodic memory buffer.

slides.title: What if an agent could learn without fine-tuning?
slides.body: Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023) reframes 'learning from a mistake' as writing a better prompt for next time, not updating a single weight.

slides.title: RL fine-tuning is overkill for 'try again, but smarter'
slides.body: Classic RL improves an agent by adjusting model weights from a reward signal — that means gradient updates, training infrastructure, and a new checkpoint per skill.
bullets: A single failed coding attempt doesn't need a training run — it needs the agent to remember what broke
Weight updates are slow, costly, and hard to do per-task or per-session
Most task failures are a specific, describable mistake, not a fundamental capability gap

slides.title: Three roles: Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection model
slides.body: Reflexion runs the same base LLM in three jobs across a retry loop, with natural language — not gradients — carrying the learning signal.
bullets: Actor: attempts the task (writes the code, picks the action, answers the question)
Evaluator: scores the trajectory — a unit test pass/fail, an exact-match check, or a heuristic
Self-Reflection model: turns a failing score into a specific verbal critique ('I used the wrong list index and never checked for an empty input')
That critique is appended to an episodic memory buffer the Actor reads on its next attempt

slides.title: The loop repeats until it passes or the memory is full
slides.body: Each trial is: act, evaluate, reflect, remember — then try again with the growing memory in context.
bullets: Trial 1: Actor attempts → Evaluator fails it → Reflection writes a note → note goes into memory
Trial 2: Actor reads memory + task, tries again with that specific mistake in view
Loop stops on success or after a fixed trial budget (the paper caps trials rather than looping forever)
Memory is capped too — old reflections get dropped or summarized so the prompt doesn't blow past the context window

slides.title: On HumanEval, one reflection loop beat the prior best
slides.body: The paper's headline result: Reflexion pushed pass@1 past a strong GPT-4 baseline on coding, with similar gains reported on decision-making and reasoning benchmarks.
bullets: Gains came from letting the same model retry with memory, not from a bigger or newer model
The paper also reports strong improvements on sequential decision-making (ALFWorld) and reasoning QA (HotPotQA) tasks, without weight updates

slides.title: Worked example: a function that fails one hidden test
slides.body: The Actor writes `find_max(nums)` that crashes on an empty list. The Evaluator runs the test suite and reports a failure on the empty-input case.
bullets: Self-Reflection writes: 'My function assumed nums is non-empty and indexed nums[0] directly — I never guarded against len(nums) == 0.'
That sentence is prepended to the next attempt's prompt, right alongside the original task
Trial 2's Actor adds an explicit empty-list check and passes — the fix came from language, not from retraining

slides.title: It only works when you can actually judge success
slides.body: Reflexion leans entirely on the Evaluator giving a trustworthy signal — take that away and the whole loop is guessing.
bullets: Needs a verifier: unit tests, exact-match answers, or a simulator reward — open-ended tasks with no ground truth get weak, unreliable reflections
Adds latency and cost: each retry is 2-3 extra LLM calls (evaluate, reflect, re-attempt) before you get a final answer
Doesn't fix a knowledge gap — if the model genuinely doesn't know the fact or algorithm, reflecting on failure won't teach it
Memory growth is a real constraint: long task chains need summarization or pruning, or reflections crowd out the actual task context

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Reflexion = Actor + Evaluator + Self-Reflection, looping on natural-language feedback instead of gradients
Failures become memory: a specific written critique the next attempt conditions on
It boosted HumanEval pass@1 from 80% to 91% over a GPT-4 baseline with zero fine-tuning
The catch: it needs a real success signal, adds retry latency, and can't teach the model something it doesn't know

questions.prompt: What actually changes between Reflexion's trial 1 and trial 2 attempts?
options: The model's weights are fine-tuned on the failed trajectory
A new, larger model is swapped in for the retry
The next attempt's prompt includes a written reflection describing the specific mistake
The task is simplified automatically before retrying
questions.explanation: Reflexion never touches model weights. The only thing that changes is the prompt: it now includes a natural-language note about exactly what went wrong, generated by the self-reflection step.

questions.prompt: Reflexion is a poor fit for which of these tasks?
options: Fixing a function that fails a specific unit test
Writing open-ended marketing copy with no defined 'correct' answer
A game-playing agent with a clear win/loss signal
A multi-hop QA task checked against an exact-match answer
questions.explanation: Reflexion depends on the Evaluator producing a trustworthy success/fail signal. Unit tests, game outcomes, and exact-match QA all give that; open-ended generation with no ground truth doesn't, so the reflections have nothing solid to critique.

questions.prompt: In the paper's reported HumanEval result, what was the pass@1 improvement from adding Reflexion to a GPT-4 baseline?
options: No measurable change
questions.explanation: The GPT-4 baseline scored 80% pass@1 on HumanEval; adding the Reflexion loop raised it to 91% — a meaningful jump from retries alone, with no retraining.

posts.title: Mage-VL: Cutting Video Tokens 75% by Reading the Codec
posts.subtitle: A 4B vision-language model that watches video the way a codec already compressed it — not frame by frame.
posts.summary: Microsoft's Mage-VL tokenizes video using the same motion vectors and residual energy a codec already computed, cutting visual tokens by over 75%. A dual-process 'System 1 / System 2' design lets a 4B model stay silent on routine footage and only reason when something response-worthy happens, beating a 15B baseline on streaming tasks.

slides.title: A 4B Model Reads Video Like a Codec, Not a Filmstrip
slides.body: Mage-VL (arXiv:2607.24904) is Microsoft's efficient, codec-native vision-language model for real-time video understanding — released July 26, 2026 alongside sibling model Mage-Flow.

slides.title: VLMs Are Great Offline, Bad at Watching Live
slides.body: The paper frames this as a 'modern Moravec's paradox': today's vision-language models ace complex offline reasoning over a handful of frames, but choke on the simple real-time task of watching a live stream.
bullets: Uniform frame sampling burns tokens on static, redundant frames
Every frame gets tokenized at the same cost, whether it's a scene cut or five seconds of stillness
That token bloat is exactly what makes long, continuous video streams too expensive to process live

slides.title: Mage-ViT: Let the Codec Tell You What Changed
slides.body: Instead of a generic ViT patch grid, Mage-ViT's custom tokenizer selectively encodes dynamic, entropy-rich regions using motion vectors and residual energy already present across sparse anchor (I) and predicted (P) frames.
bullets: Cuts visual token consumption by over 75% vs. uniform frame sampling
Preserves spatiotemporal context instead of discarding it wholesale
Trained from scratch on ~560M unlabeled images + 100M unlabeled video frames
16×16 patch grid with 3D rotary position encoding on a Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 language backbone

slides.title: System 1 Watches Silently, System 2 Only Speaks Up When It Matters
slides.body: A lightweight 'cognition gate' (System 1) monitors each rolling codec window and stays silent on routine content. It invokes the full VLM (System 2) only when a response-worthy event completes.
bullets: System 1: cheap, always-on gate scanning the compressed stream
System 2: the full Qwen3-4B-backed VLM, invoked selectively
Token savings compound: fewer visual tokens per frame, and full reasoning skipped on 'nothing happened' stretches
Enables training on 8× longer videos under the same compute budget

slides.title: 4B Params, Beats a 15B Baseline on Video
slides.body: Mage-VL-4B matches Qwen3-VL-4B on static image tasks while pulling ahead on video and spatial benchmarks, and comprehensively surpasses the 15B Phi-4-Reasoning-Vision baseline.

slides.title: A Livestream Assistant That Doesn't Narrate Dead Air
slides.body: On SoccerNet-style streaming benchmarks, Mage-VL is scored on catching notable moments in a live feed rather than describing every frame.
bullets: Feed: a continuous soccer broadcast, compressed as a normal video codec stream
System 1 stays quiet through routine midfield play — no tokens spent, no response generated
The moment a goal-scoring sequence completes, System 2 wakes up and reports it
Streaming eval: TimVal 55.54, F1 16.35, ROC-AUC 83.14 on SoccerNet

slides.title: Where It Doesn't Apply
slides.body: The efficiency gains are tied directly to codec structure, and the training recipe makes a deliberate tradeoff.
bullets: Needs access to compressed-stream metadata (motion vectors, I/P frames) — not a drop-in replacement for pipelines that only see raw decoded frames
Less advantage on a single static image, where there's no temporal redundancy to exploit
Five-stage supervised curriculum only — no RLHF or preference tuning, which can leave subjective response quality behind RLHF'd competitors
Trained at a fixed 4B budget for research access, not tuned as a maximal-quality flagship

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Mage-VL tokenizes video using signals the codec already computed, not a generic uniform sampler
A dual-process design (silent gate + full VLM) turns 'watch everything' into 'react only when needed'
Result: a 4B model beats a 15B baseline on streaming video understanding, at up to 3.5× the speed
Tradeoff: it trades RLHF polish and raw-frame generality for codec-native efficiency

questions.prompt: What signal does Mage-ViT's tokenizer use to decide which video regions to encode in detail?
options: A fixed uniform grid applied to every frame equally
Motion vectors and residual energy already present in the video codec's I/P frames
Random sampling of pixels per frame
Manual human-labeled regions of interest
questions.explanation: Mage-ViT reuses the motion vectors and residual energy the codec already computed across anchor (I) and predicted (P) frames, so it can selectively encode dynamic, entropy-rich regions instead of tokenizing every pixel uniformly.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of Mage-VL's 'System 1 / System 2' design?
options: To run two full VLMs in parallel for redundancy
To let a cheap always-on gate stay silent on routine footage, invoking the full model only when something response-worthy happens
To alternate between image mode and video mode
To split training into two separate datasets
questions.explanation: System 1 is a lightweight cognition gate that watches the rolling codec window and stays quiet during routine content; System 2, the full VLM, is invoked only when a response-worthy event completes — avoiding wasted compute on dead air.

questions.prompt: What did Mage-VL's authors skip that most competitive VLMs include?
options: Any video training data
A visual encoder
RLHF or preference-based post-training — it uses only a five-stage supervised curriculum
Position encoding
questions.explanation: Mage-VL is trained with a five-stage supervised curriculum (captions, instructions, temporal grounding) and no RLHF or preference/RL post-training — a deliberate efficiency tradeoff that can leave subjective response quality behind RLHF'd rivals.

posts.title: A2A: How AI Agents From Different Vendors Talk to Each Other
posts.subtitle: MCP connects an agent to its tools. A2A connects one agent to another — even one it's never met.
posts.summary: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol, now under Linux Foundation governance, that lets independent AI agents — built on different frameworks, hosted by different companies — discover each other and collaborate on tasks. It's complementary to MCP: MCP wires an agent to its tools; A2A wires agents to each other.

slides.title: Two Agents, Two Vendors, One Protocol
slides.body: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open, Apache-2.0 protocol originally contributed by Google, now governed by the Linux Foundation, that reached v1.0 in 2026.

slides.title: MCP Solves Tools. It Doesn't Solve Agent-to-Agent.
slides.body: Model Context Protocol standardizes how a single agent connects to its own tools and data — a vertical connection. It says nothing about how a LangChain-based agent should call a CrewAI-based agent hosted by a different company.
bullets: Before A2A, cross-vendor agent collaboration meant bespoke, one-off integrations
Every pair of frameworks needed its own glue code and auth handling
None of it was discoverable — you had to already know the other agent's API

slides.title: The Agent Card: How an Agent Introduces Itself
slides.body: Any A2A-compliant agent publishes a JSON manifest at a well-known URL, before any task ever starts.
bullets: Published at /.well-known/agent-card.json on the agent's endpoint
Declares the agent's name, version, skills, supported content types, and required auth schemes
Lets a caller discover what an unfamiliar agent can do and how to authenticate — no prior integration needed

slides.title: Tasks Have a Lifecycle, Not Just a Response
slides.body: Work is framed as a Task with defined states, not a single request/response — because agent work can be long-running, need human input mid-flight, or fail partway through.
bullets: 8 task states: submitted, working, input_required, auth_required, completed, failed, canceled, rejected
Transport: JSON-RPC 2.0 (also gRPC / HTTP+JSON bindings)
Server-Sent Events stream live progress instead of forcing the caller to poll
Webhook push notifications let a caller walk away and be notified when a long task finishes

slides.title: A2A vs. MCP: Different Layers, Not Competitors

rows: Delegate work to another org's agent

slides.title: Delegating a Booking Step to Someone Else's Agent
slides.body: A travel-orchestrator agent needs seat selection handled by the airline's own specialized agent, which it has never integrated with before.
bullets: It fetches the airline agent's Agent Card to learn its skills and auth requirements
It submits a Task with the request as a structured message Part
It subscribes over SSE and watches the state move: submitted → working
The airline agent flips to input_required to ask for a passport number, then completed with a booking artifact once done
The orchestrator never needed to know how the airline's agent was built internally

slides.title: When Not to Reach for A2A
slides.body: The task-lifecycle machinery and cross-org auth are real complexity — worth paying only when you're actually crossing an agent or vendor boundary.
bullets: A single app calling its own internal tools should just use MCP or plain function calling
Overkill for two agents you control and can integrate directly
Ecosystem and tooling are thinner than MCP's — it only reached v1.0 in 2026
Cross-org auth (auth_required state, security schemes) still requires real coordination, not just protocol compliance

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A2A standardizes agent-to-agent discovery and delegation across vendors — MCP standardizes agent-to-tool access
Discovery starts with an Agent Card at a well-known URL, before any task begins
Tasks are stateful (8 lifecycle states) with SSE streaming and webhook push, built for long-running async work
The two protocols compose: an A2A agent typically uses MCP internally to call its own tools

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between what MCP and A2A each standardize?
options: They do the same thing; A2A is just a newer version of MCP
MCP standardizes agent-to-tool/data connections; A2A standardizes agent-to-agent collaboration across vendors
MCP is for video models, A2A is for text models
A2A replaces HTTP entirely
questions.explanation: MCP is a vertical connection — one agent to its own tools and data. A2A is horizontal — independent agents, possibly built on different frameworks by different companies, discovering and delegating work to each other.

questions.prompt: Where does an A2A agent publish the manifest that lets other agents discover its capabilities?
options: In a private database only the agent's own team can query
At a well-known URL: /.well-known/agent-card.json
It emails the manifest to any agent that asks
There is no discovery mechanism; integrations are always manual
questions.explanation: The Agent Card is a JSON manifest published at /.well-known/agent-card.json, declaring the agent's skills, supported content types, and auth requirements — so an unfamiliar caller can discover what it does before starting a task.

questions.prompt: Why does A2A model work as a stateful Task with multiple lifecycle states instead of a single request/response?
options: To make the protocol harder to implement
Because agent work can be long-running, may need mid-flight human input, and can fail partway — states like input_required and auth_required capture that
Because JSON-RPC requires at least 8 states
States are purely cosmetic and have no functional purpose
questions.explanation: A single response can't represent work that pauses for a passport number, requires authentication partway through, or runs for minutes. The 8-state lifecycle (including input_required and auth_required) plus SSE/webhooks lets callers track and react to that without polling.

posts.title: DPO: Skipping RLHF's Reward Model Entirely
posts.subtitle: Turn chosen-vs-rejected pairs into a classification loss on the policy itself — no reward model, no PPO rollouts, no critic.
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) reframes RLHF's reward-model-plus-PPO pipeline as a single supervised loss over chosen/rejected response pairs. By showing the optimal RLHF policy has a closed-form relationship to the reward function, DPO trains directly on preference data — no reward model, no rollouts, no critic — at the cost of losing PPO's online exploration.

slides.title: One Loss Function Instead of a Whole RL Pipeline
slides.body: DPO, introduced by Rafailov et al. in 2023, proved that RLHF's reward model is mathematically redundant — the same alignment signal can be extracted with a single classification-style loss.
bullets: Standard RLHF needs 3 stages: supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, then PPO reinforcement learning against that reward model
DPO collapses stages 2 and 3 into one supervised step run directly on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples
No reward model to train, no rollouts to sample, no PPO instability — just gradient descent on log-probabilities

slides.title: RLHF's Pipeline Is Expensive and Fragile
slides.body: Classic RLHF keeps four models in memory at once and tunes PPO's famously touchy hyperparameters.
bullets: A policy, a frozen reference policy, a reward model, and (in PPO) a value network — four model copies live in GPU memory simultaneously
The reward model is trained once, then frozen and reused as a proxy — if it's exploitable, PPO will find and abuse the exploit (reward hacking)
PPO's clipping, GAE, and KL coefficients each need tuning per task; runs can silently collapse or diverge partway through training

slides.title: The Optimal Policy IS a Reward Model
slides.body: DPO's key derivation: for the standard RLHF objective (maximize reward minus a KL penalty from the reference model), the optimal policy has a closed-form solution in terms of the reward. Invert that relationship, and any reward function can be rewritten purely in terms of policy log-probabilities.
bullets: Substituting that inverted reward into the Bradley-Terry preference model produces a loss defined entirely on the policy and reference model — the reward model cancels out algebraically
Loss: -log σ( β·[log(π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x)) − log(π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x))] ), where y_w is the chosen response and y_l the rejected one
β controls how far the policy is allowed to drift from the reference model — small β allows bigger updates, large β keeps outputs conservative
The loss just pushes the chosen response's relative log-probability up and the rejected one's down — no sampling, no rollouts required

slides.title: What You Actually Need to Train It
bullets: A frozen reference model (usually the SFT checkpoint) — its log-probs anchor the KL term implicitly, no separate KL computation needed
A policy model, initialized from the same SFT checkpoint, that you're actively updating
A static preference dataset: (prompt, chosen response, rejected response) triples — collected once, no online generation
Per training step: two forward passes each on chosen and rejected text (policy + frozen reference), then backprop the DPO loss — that's the entire training loop

slides.title: RLHF/PPO vs. DPO

rows: Can generate and score novel responses
Limited to patterns already in the dataset

slides.title: One Preference Pair, Worked Through
slides.body: A concrete pass through a single training example.
bullets: Prompt: 'Explain quantum entanglement to a 5-year-old.' Chosen: a short, playful analogy. Rejected: a dense paragraph full of jargon.
Forward pass computes log-probabilities under the policy and the reference for both responses; initially policy ≈ reference, so the bracketed term ≈ 0 and loss ≈ -log σ(0) = log 2

The gradient step raises the chosen response's log-probability and lowers the rejected one's relative to the frozen reference — the model learns 'more like this, less like that' without ever seeing a numeric reward
Repeat over tens of thousands of pairs and the policy shifts toward the chosen style broadly, not just on the exact prompts seen

slides.title: Where DPO Breaks Down
slides.body: The simplicity has real costs, not just savings.
bullets: Likelihood displacement: DPO can end up lowering the probability of BOTH the chosen and rejected response, as long as the gap between them grows — sometimes pushing probability mass elsewhere in the vocabulary unpredictably
It's fully offline: unlike PPO's online rollouts, DPO only ever sees the preference pairs you collected — it can't discover and reinforce a better response you never wrote down
Overfits fast: because it's a comparatively simple classification loss, a handful of epochs at too-high a learning rate can degrade generation quality even as the loss keeps dropping
β is a real hyperparameter to tune per dataset — too low and the policy drifts and destabilizes, too high and preference updates barely move the model

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: DPO reframes RLHF as a single supervised loss: it exploits a closed-form link between the optimal RLHF policy and the reward function so the reward model cancels out algebraically
Training only needs a policy model and a frozen reference model — no reward model, no PPO rollouts, no value network
It trades PPO's online exploration for offline simplicity — output quality is capped by how good your existing preference dataset is
Watch for likelihood displacement and overfitting: DPO's loss can keep falling while output quality degrades if not carefully monitored

questions.prompt: What mathematical trick lets DPO skip training a separate reward model?
options: It uses a pretrained sentiment classifier as the reward model instead
It shows the optimal RLHF policy has a closed-form relation to the reward, so the reward model cancels out and becomes a function of policy log-probabilities
It replaces the reward model with a majority vote across multiple sampled completions
It removes the KL penalty entirely, making a reward model unnecessary
questions.explanation: DPO's derivation inverts the closed-form solution for the optimal KL-constrained RLHF policy, substitutes it into the Bradley-Terry preference model, and finds the reward model term cancels out — leaving a loss defined purely on the policy's own log-probabilities relative to a frozen reference.

questions.prompt: In the DPO loss, what does the hyperparameter β control?
options: The learning rate used for the optimizer
The number of preference pairs sampled per batch
How far the policy is allowed to drift from the reference model before the loss penalizes it
The temperature used when generating the chosen/rejected responses
questions.explanation: β scales the implicit KL penalty against the reference model. A small β permits large policy updates (higher drift risk); a large β keeps the policy conservative but slows how much the preference signal moves it.

questions.prompt: What is 'likelihood displacement,' a known failure mode of DPO?
options: The reward model assigns high reward to both responses equally
DPO can lower the probability of both the chosen and rejected response, as long as the gap between them widens, sometimes pushing probability mass elsewhere in the vocabulary
The reference model's weights drift during training even though they should stay frozen
PPO's value network fails to converge on the same dataset
questions.explanation: Because the loss only cares about the log-probability gap between chosen and rejected, DPO can satisfy it by pushing down both probabilities rather than pushing up the chosen one — a documented degeneracy that requires careful learning-rate and epoch control to avoid.

posts.title: Continuous Batching: No More Waiting for the Slowest Request
posts.subtitle: How iteration-level scheduling keeps every GPU slot busy
posts.summary: Continuous batching schedules LLM inference at the token-generation step instead of the whole-request level, so a finished sequence's GPU slot is handed to a new request immediately rather than sitting idle until the slowest sequence in the batch finishes. It's what lets servers like vLLM and TGI keep GPUs busy under mixed, unpredictable request lengths, at the cost of more complex scheduling and new latency-interference tradeoffs.

slides.title: One Slow Request Can Stall an Entire Batch
slides.body: Batch 8 requests together to keep a GPU busy, and by default the batch can't return anything until every sequence in it is done — even if 7 of them finished generating 50 tokens ago and are just waiting on the 8th to reach 2,000.

slides.title: Static Batching Schedules at the Wrong Granularity
slides.body: Classic request-level (static) batching locks a set of sequences together for the batch's entire lifetime. The scheduler decides once, at admission time, which requests share a GPU pass — and can't change that decision until all of them finish.
bullets: Output lengths vary wildly per request, so the batch's total latency is set by whichever sequence takes longest to hit its stop token
A finished sequence's compute slot and KV cache sit idle instead of being reassigned — wasted GPU cycles that could serve a new arrival
New requests queue behind the whole batch even if there's spare capacity mid-batch, so tail latency grows with traffic variance, not just load
Padding short sequences up to the batch's max length wastes both compute and memory on tokens that don't exist

slides.title: Schedule Every Iteration, Not Every Request
slides.body: Continuous batching (also called iteration-level or in-flight batching) reruns the scheduling decision after every single decode step — not once per request. The moment any sequence in the running batch emits a stop token, its slot is freed and the scheduler can immediately admit a queued request into that same forward pass.
bullets: The unit of scheduling shrinks from 'a whole generation' to 'one token step for the whole batch'
Each request keeps its own independent KV cache, so mixing sequences at different stages in the same batched matmul is safe — they just occupy different rows
Newly admitted requests first go through a prefill step for their prompt, then join the shared decode loop alongside sequences already mid-generation
GPU occupancy tracks actual work in flight instead of the batch's slowest member, which is the main source of the throughput gain

slides.title: Two Phases Competing for the Same GPU
slides.body: Continuous batching has to interleave two very different kinds of work every iteration: prefill (processing a new prompt, compute-bound, scales with prompt length) and decode (generating one token per active sequence, memory-bandwidth-bound). Naively injecting a large prefill into a decode-heavy batch stalls every in-flight sequence for that step.
bullets: Systems like vLLM and TGI pair continuous batching with paged KV cache management so admitting a new sequence doesn't require a contiguous memory allocation
Chunked prefill splits a long prompt's prefill across several iterations, interleaved with ongoing decode steps, so one big prompt doesn't freeze everyone else's next token
The scheduler typically caps batch size by KV cache memory, not just request count — admission stops once the cache pool is full, regardless of queue depth
Request order in the batch is fluid: it's re-decided every iteration based on who's finished, who's arrived, and what memory is free

slides.title: Static vs. Continuous Batching
slides.body: The shapes of the tradeoff, independent of any specific benchmark numbers:

rows: Low — slots refill as they free

slides.title: Worked Example: Eight Requests, Wildly Different Lengths
slides.body: A batch admits 8 chat requests. Six are short replies (~30 tokens). One is a long code generation (~1,500 tokens). One is a short factual answer (~15 tokens) that arrives 200ms after the batch starts.
bullets: Static batching: the batch can't return anything until the 1,500-token sequence finishes — the six short replies sit fully generated but unreturned, and the late arrival queues behind the entire batch

Continuous batching: each short reply is returned the moment it hits its stop token, freeing its slot within one iteration; the late arrival is admitted into the very next decode step instead of waiting in a queue
The 1,500-token sequence still takes just as long in both cases — continuous batching doesn't speed up any single sequence, it stops that sequence from blocking everyone else's

slides.title: Where It Bites: Interference and Fairness
slides.body: Continuous batching trades a simple scheduling model for a harder one, and that complexity shows up as new failure modes rather than eliminating old ones.
bullets: A newly admitted long prompt's prefill chunk still consumes a step's compute budget, which can add a visible latency blip to sequences already mid-decode in that batch
Without a fairness policy, a flood of short requests can keep re-filling slots and effectively starve a long-running sequence of throughput share
The per-iteration scheduler itself has CPU/host overhead — at very low request volume, that overhead can outweigh the benefit static batching would have given for free
It only helps when request lengths and arrival times actually vary; a workload with uniform, synchronized-length requests gains little because static batching wasn't leaving much idle time to reclaim

slides.title: Reschedule Every Step, Not Every Request
bullets: Static batching wastes GPU capacity because it can't reassign a finished sequence's slot until the entire batch is done
Continuous batching re-decides the batch's membership after every decode step, admitting new requests the instant a slot frees
It depends on paged, non-contiguous KV cache management to admit/evict sequences cheaply, and on chunked prefill to keep new prompts from stalling in-flight decodes
It doesn't make any single request faster — it removes the idle time other requests used to cause, which is why it mainly pays off under mixed, bursty, variable-length traffic

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between static (request-level) batching and continuous batching?
options: Continuous batching uses a bigger batch size
Continuous batching re-schedules which requests share the GPU after every decode step, not once per whole request
Static batching runs on CPU while continuous batching runs on GPU
Continuous batching skips the prefill phase entirely
questions.explanation: The distinguishing idea is scheduling granularity: static batching locks a group of requests together until all finish, while continuous batching re-evaluates batch membership at every single token step, letting finished sequences exit and new ones enter immediately.

questions.prompt: Why does continuous batching typically require a paged (non-contiguous) KV cache instead of a simple contiguous buffer per batch slot?
options: Paging makes each individual token's attention computation faster
Requests enter and leave the batch constantly, so memory needs to be allocated and freed in small chunks rather than reserved as one fixed contiguous block per request
It's required by the model architecture itself, unrelated to batching
Contiguous memory can't be used with GPUs at all
questions.explanation: Since sequences join and leave the running batch every iteration, reserving one large contiguous KV buffer per slot up front (sized for a worst-case length) would waste memory and make admitting/evicting requests expensive. Paged KV cache lets memory be allocated in fixed-size blocks as needed, which is what makes cheap per-step admission practical.

questions.prompt: A new long prompt gets admitted into a batch that's mid-decode on several other sequences. What's the known downside?
options: The new prompt's prefill step can add a latency blip to the sequences already decoding in that same iteration
The other sequences immediately lose their KV cache and must restart
The GPU automatically rejects the new request until the batch is empty
There is no downside — this is exactly the intended fast path with zero cost
questions.explanation: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so mixing them in one iteration means the prefill chunk competes for that step's compute budget, which can visibly delay the in-flight decode sequences. This is why systems use chunked prefill — splitting a long prompt's prefill across several iterations — to soften the interference rather than eliminate it.

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Paying Once for Context You Reuse a Thousand Times
posts.subtitle: Why the same system prompt shouldn't cost the same tokens every single call
posts.summary: Prompt caching reuses the already-computed attention state (KV cache) for a shared prefix across requests, so a long system prompt, tool schema, or document only gets fully processed once instead of on every call. It cuts latency and cost dramatically on cache hits, but only works when the prefix is byte-identical up to the cache point and requests land inside a short TTL window.

slides.title: The Same 4,000 Tokens, Recomputed Every Single Call
slides.body: An agent with a long system prompt, a tool schema, and a style guide re-sends and re-processes that entire prefix on every request — even when nothing in it changed since the last call.

slides.title: Prefill Cost Scales With Every Token You Send, Not Just the New Ones
slides.body: Before a model generates its first output token, it must run a forward pass over the entire input — the 'prefill' phase. A chatbot with a 3,000-token system prompt plus a 500-token user turn pays for all 3,500 tokens of compute, every message, even though 3,000 of them are identical to the last call.
bullets: Long system prompts, tool/function schemas, and few-shot examples are the worst offenders — static, large, and repeated verbatim on every call
Multi-turn agents resend the whole growing transcript each turn, so prefill cost grows linearly with conversation length
This shows up as both wasted spend and added latency before the model even starts responding

slides.title: The Fix: Cache the KV State of a Shared Prefix, Not Just the Text
slides.body: During prefill, the model computes key/value tensors for every input token — the same KV cache used to speed up generation. Prompt caching persists that KV state server-side, keyed to the exact prefix, so a later request sharing that prefix can skip recomputing it and jump straight to the new tokens.
bullets: You mark a 'cache breakpoint' after the stable part of the prompt (system instructions, tool defs, a large retrieved document)
A cache hit requires the prefix to match byte-for-byte up to that point — one changed word invalidates everything after it
Only the tokens after the breakpoint (the new user turn) go through full prefill; the cached prefix is loaded, not recomputed
Caches are short-lived (typically minutes, not hours) and evicted under memory pressure, so this is a latency/cost optimization, not durable storage

slides.title: Worked Example: A Coding Agent With a 6K-Token System Prompt
slides.body: An agent's system prompt (repo conventions, tool schemas, coding guidelines) is 6,000 tokens. The user's actual question is 200 tokens. Across a 20-turn debugging session, that 6,000-token prefix would normally be reprocessed 20 times.
bullets: Without caching: 20 calls × 6,000 shared tokens = 120,000 tokens of redundant prefill, all billed at full input price
With caching: the prefix is written to cache once on turn 1; turns 2-20 pay a small cache-read cost for those 6,000 tokens instead of full price, plus full price only for the new 200-token turn
The savings compound fastest in agent loops and RAG pipelines where a large static block (tools, retrieved docs) precedes a small dynamic block (the actual question)

slides.title: Cache Write vs. Cache Read vs. No Cache
slides.body: Providers differ on exact multipliers, but the shape is consistent across major LLM APIs: writing to the cache costs a small premium over a normal token, while reading from it costs a small fraction of a normal token.

rows: Every call, prefix reprocessed from scratch
First call, or first call after the cache expired
Any call within the TTL that repeats the same prefix

slides.title: Where It Breaks: Invalidation and Idle Gaps
slides.body: Prompt caching is fragile in ways that surprise teams who bolt it on without restructuring their prompts.
bullets: Any edit before the breakpoint — a timestamp, a reordered tool, an interpolated variable — invalidates the cache for everything after it
Putting volatile content (current date, user ID, session token) early in the prompt silently kills your hit rate; it belongs after the cache breakpoint, not before it
The cache has a short TTL, so a bursty workload with gaps longer than that window pays full price on every 'first' request again
Caching doesn't help when every request's prefix is genuinely unique (e.g., a different large document per call) — there's nothing to reuse

slides.title: Structure Prompts Stable-First, Volatile-Last
bullets: Prompt caching reuses a prefix's computed KV state instead of recomputing it, cutting both latency and cost on repeated calls
It requires an exact prefix match up to the cache breakpoint — order matters: put static content (system prompt, tools, docs) first, dynamic content (user turn, timestamps) last
It shines in agent loops, multi-turn chat, and RAG with large retrieved context — anywhere a big static block precedes a small dynamic one
It does nothing for genuinely unique, single-use prompts, and a cold cache (first call, or after the TTL lapses) pays a small write premium, not a discount

questions.prompt: What does prompt caching actually persist between requests?
options: The raw text of the prompt, compressed
The model's computed KV (key/value) state for a shared prefix
A summary of the conversation generated by the model
The final output tokens from the previous call
questions.explanation: Caching stores the KV tensors computed during prefill for a given prefix, so a later request with the same prefix can reuse that state instead of recomputing it — the same underlying KV cache used during generation, just persisted across calls.

questions.prompt: You add the current timestamp to the very start of your system prompt, before your tool definitions. What happens to your cache hit rate?
options: No effect — only the last 100 tokens matter for caching
It improves, since timestamps help the cache key be more specific
It collapses toward zero, since the changing timestamp invalidates everything that follows it
It only affects cost, not whether the cache hits
questions.explanation: A cache hit requires the prefix to match exactly up to the breakpoint. A timestamp that changes every call breaks the match immediately, so everything after it — including your large, otherwise-stable tool definitions — is invalidated too. Volatile content belongs after the cache breakpoint, not before it.

questions.prompt: For which workload does prompt caching provide the LEAST benefit?
options: A coding agent reusing the same 6,000-token system prompt across 20 turns
A RAG pipeline that stuffs a large, unchanging retrieved document into every call in a session
A batch job where every request has a completely different, one-off large document as its prefix
A customer support bot with a fixed style guide and tool schema
questions.explanation: Caching only pays off when a prefix is reused across multiple calls. If every request's large content is unique, there's no shared prefix to reuse — the cache write premium is paid every time with no matching read to offset it.

posts.title: Tokenization: How BPE Turns Text Into the Units a Model Actually Sees
posts.subtitle: An LLM never reads letters or words — it reads a vocabulary of a few hundred thousand learned chunks
posts.summary: Before any text reaches an LLM's weights, a tokenizer chops it into subword pieces from a fixed vocabulary using Byte-Pair Encoding — merging the most frequent adjacent pairs over and over until the vocab hits a target size. That single design choice explains why LLMs mangle letter-counting, charge more for some languages than others, and occasionally spit out gibberish on rare 'glitch tokens.'

slides.title: The Model Never Sees a Single Letter
slides.body: Every LLM interaction starts with a step most users never think about: a tokenizer converts your text into a sequence of integers before a single weight gets multiplied. Those integers index into a fixed vocabulary of subword chunks — not letters, not always whole words.

slides.title: Why Not Just Use Characters or Words?
slides.body: Both obvious choices break down at scale, for opposite reasons.
bullets: Character-level tokenization keeps the vocabulary tiny (~100-200 symbols) but makes sequences extremely long — a 500-word article becomes thousands of tokens, and the model has to learn spelling before it can learn meaning.

Whole-word tokenization keeps sequences short but the vocabulary explodes: every inflection, typo, and compound needs its own slot, and any word missing from training becomes an unrepresentable 'unknown' token.

Real text also mixes languages, code, emoji, and numbers — a fixed word list can't cover all of it, but you still need a bounded vocabulary so the model's embedding table stays a finite, trainable size.
The fix subword tokenization lands on: build a vocabulary of frequently-occurring chunks — common words stay whole, rare words split into pieces, so nothing is ever truly 'unknown.'

slides.title: Byte-Pair Encoding: Merge the Most Common Pair, Repeat
slides.body: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE), and its close relatives WordPiece and SentencePiece's unigram model, build the vocabulary by starting small and growing it through repeated merges.
bullets: Start with every individual byte or character as its own token — the smallest possible vocabulary.
Scan the entire training corpus and find the single most frequent adjacent pair of tokens (e.g. 't' + 'h' appearing constantly) and merge it into one new token 'th'.
Repeat: re-scan, find the new most frequent adjacent pair (now possibly 'th' + 'e' → 'the'), merge again — each round adds exactly one new vocabulary entry.

Stop once the vocabulary hits a target size (GPT-style tokenizers commonly land in the 100K-200K range) — the result is a mix of full common words, frequent subwords, and single bytes for anything rare.

slides.title: Vocabulary Size Is a Real Engineering Tradeoff
slides.body: Picking the target vocabulary size trades off three things that all cost money or latency.
bullets: Bigger vocabulary → shorter token sequences for the same text, which means less compute per request and more text fitting in a fixed context window.
Bigger vocabulary → a bigger embedding table and output softmax layer, since both scale linearly with vocab size — that's parameters and memory spent before the model does any 'thinking.'
Smaller vocabulary → longer sequences, so the same context window (say 128K tokens) holds less actual text — a real cost since attention compute grows with sequence length.

This is exactly why newer tokenizers (like OpenAI's o200k_base, roughly 200K tokens, versus the older cl100k_base's ~100K) trend larger over time: more vocabulary buys shorter sequences, which is worth the bigger embedding table at scale.

slides.title: Worked Example: Watching a Word Get Split
slides.body: Common English words are usually a single token. Everything else reveals the merge history.
bullets: 'the', 'and', 'is' — each one whole token, because they're among the most frequent strings in any English corpus, so BPE merged them all the way down early.
'tokenization' commonly splits into pieces like 'token' + 'ization' — frequent enough as sub-parts to merge, not frequent enough as a whole word to earn its own single token.

A rare or invented word, a typo, or a string in a low-resource language can fall all the way back to individual bytes — which is why the SAME sentence can cost noticeably more tokens (and more money, since APIs bill per token) in one language than another.

Numbers are especially telling: '2026' might be one token, while a long number like '48291035' often splits into multiple 3-digit chunks — which is a big part of why LLMs are unreliable at multi-digit arithmetic without help.

slides.title: Character vs. Word vs. Subword
slides.body: Subword tokenization is the compromise every modern LLM converges on.
bullets: None of these is free — subword tokenization just sits at the point on the curve that's cheapest to train and serve at scale.

rows: Yes — falls back to smaller pieces

slides.title: Where Tokenization Bites You
slides.body: Because the model reasons over tokens, not characters, tokenization leaks into behavior in ways that look like model bugs but are actually tokenizer artifacts.
bullets: Letter-counting and spelling tasks ('how many r's in strawberry') are hard for LLMs precisely because the model may never see 'strawberry' as individual letters — it sees one or two opaque tokens and has to infer spelling indirectly from training data.

'Glitch tokens' — rare tokens that appeared in the tokenizer's training data but almost never in the model's actual training text — can produce erratic output when they do show up, because the model never learned a stable representation for them.

A tokenizer trained on mostly-English data assigns more tokens per word to other languages, so the same sentence can cost 2-3x more tokens (and money, and context budget) in a lower-resource language.

Swapping or fine-tuning a tokenizer after a model is trained is essentially impossible without retraining — the vocabulary is baked into the embedding table, so tokenizer choice is a decision made once, early, and lived with forever.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Tokenizers split text into subword units from a fixed vocabulary, built by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair (BPE) until hitting a target size.
Vocabulary size is a real tradeoff: bigger vocab means shorter sequences and less compute per request, at the cost of a bigger embedding table.
Because the model reasons over tokens, not letters, tasks like spelling, letter-counting, and multi-digit arithmetic are structurally harder than they look.

Tokenizer choice is fixed at training time and directly affects cost — the same text can be cheaper or more expensive to process depending on how well the tokenizer's training data matched the language you're using.

questions.prompt: What does Byte-Pair Encoding do, at its core, to build a vocabulary?
options: It assigns a unique token to every dictionary word in advance
It repeatedly finds the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens in the training corpus and merges it into a new single token, until the vocabulary reaches a target size
It splits every word into a fixed number of characters
It randomly samples substrings from the training data to fill the vocabulary
questions.explanation: BPE starts from individual bytes/characters and grows the vocabulary one merge at a time, always merging whichever adjacent pair is currently most frequent. That's why common words end up as single tokens while rare strings stay split into smaller pieces.

questions.prompt: Why do LLMs often struggle to count the letters in a word like 'strawberry'?
options: They have no training data about spelling
The tokenizer may represent the whole word (or large chunks of it) as one opaque token, so the model never directly sees the individual letters
Letter-counting requires more parameters than any current model has
It's a deliberate safety restriction
questions.explanation: The model computes over token embeddings, not characters. If 'strawberry' is one or two tokens, the letter-by-letter structure isn't explicitly present in the input the model reasons over — any spelling knowledge has to be learned indirectly.

questions.prompt: Why does a bigger tokenizer vocabulary (e.g. 200K vs. 100K tokens) generally make serving an LLM cheaper?
options: It doesn't — bigger vocabularies always increase cost
It shortens the average number of tokens needed to represent the same text, reducing compute per request and freeing up context window, at the cost of a larger embedding table
It removes the need for an embedding table entirely
It makes the model file size smaller
questions.explanation: More vocabulary entries mean more text can be represented in fewer tokens, and since attention compute scales with sequence length, shorter token sequences are cheaper to process — the tradeoff is a bigger (but fixed, one-time) embedding table.

posts.title: Constrained Decoding: Making Invalid JSON Impossible, Not Just Unlikely
posts.subtitle: How grammars turn 'please output valid JSON' from a request into a guarantee
posts.summary: Constrained decoding masks invalid tokens at every generation step using a compiled grammar (JSON Schema, regex, or GBNF), guaranteeing syntactically valid structured output by construction instead of by probability. It kills the parsing-failure class of bugs entirely, but it has no opinion on whether the content is true — so it's best paired with reasoning-first prompting and downstream validation.

slides.title: The Model Can Only Say What the Grammar Allows
slides.body: Constrained decoding turns 'please respond in JSON' from a polite request into a mathematical guarantee — by editing the model's choices at generation time, not its intentions.

slides.title: Free-Text Generation Breaks Tool-Calling Pipelines
slides.body: An LLM samples one token at a time from its entire vocabulary. Nothing stops it from writing a stray comment, an unescaped quote, or a trailing comma — and a downstream JSON.parse() only needs one wrong character to throw.
bullets: Prompting harder ('ONLY return valid JSON, no other text') reduces failures but never eliminates them
Retry-until-it-parses loops burn extra tokens and latency, and still fail occasionally at scale
Fine-tuning on formatted examples nudges style but is a learned habit, not an enforced rule

slides.title: Mask Every Token That Would Break the Grammar
slides.body: At each decoding step, the constraint engine tracks which grammar state the output is currently in, computes the set of vocabulary tokens that keep it valid, and sets every other token's logit to -infinity before sampling.
bullets: The grammar is compiled from a spec — JSON Schema, a regex, or a formal grammar — into an automaton (FSM or CFG)
Sampling still picks among the valid tokens by probability, so style and word choice stay flexible inside the allowed shape
llama.cpp's GBNF format defines this with production rules, e.g. root ::= object, object ::= "{" pair ("," pair)* "}"
The guarantee is structural: the automaton cannot emit an out-of-grammar token, so syntactic validity is 100% by construction, not by probability

slides.title: Walking a Tool Call Token by Token
slides.body: Say a weather-agent schema requires {"name": string, "args": {"city": string}}. After the model emits {"name", the automaton only allows a colon next — every other token in the vocabulary is masked to -infinity, no matter how probable the model thinks some other token is.
bullets: After the colon, the only valid token class is a JSON string opener (a quote) — numbers or braces get masked out
Once inside the string, any character is legal until an unescaped quote closes it — the grammar narrows and widens as it walks the schema tree
Libraries like Outlines precompile a regex/FSM index so this mask lookup is a fast table read, not a fresh automaton walk every token

slides.title: Three Ways to Get Structured Output

rows: None — fails some % of the time

slides.title: It Guarantees Shape, Never Truth
slides.body: Constrained decoding only restricts syntax. A perfectly-shaped JSON tool call can still hallucinate a city that doesn't exist or invent a field value — the grammar has no opinion on whether the content is correct.
bullets: Constraining too early can hurt reasoning: forcing structure onto a chain-of-thought before the model has 'thought' can lock in a bad answer — best practice is to reason freely, then constrain only the final answer
Grammar compilation has a one-time cost per schema (building the FSM/index) — cache and reuse it across requests with the same schema instead of recompiling per call
Deeply nested or highly recursive schemas can slow per-token mask computation on very large vocabularies
It doesn't replace validating business logic — still check that a returned city is real, that a date isn't in the past, and so on

slides.title: Constrain the Shape, Not the Thinking
bullets: Constrained decoding masks invalid tokens at generation time — the model literally cannot produce a token outside the grammar
It's implemented via compiled automatons: GBNF grammars in llama.cpp, regex/FSM indexes in libraries like Outlines, JSON Schema in most vendor 'structured output' modes
It eliminates the parsing-failure class of bugs entirely, but does nothing for hallucinated content — pair it with validation
Best practice: let the model reason unconstrained, then apply the grammar only to the final structured answer

questions.prompt: What exactly does constrained decoding guarantee?
options: That the output values are factually correct
That the output always matches the grammar's syntax
That the model reasons better before answering
That the response is shorter
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding masks every token that would violate the grammar, so the output is syntactically guaranteed to parse — but the grammar has no way to check whether the content itself (a city name, a number) is true.

questions.prompt: How does the mechanism actually stop an invalid token from being generated?
options: It fine-tunes the model weights ahead of time
It re-prompts the model to try again after a failure
It sets the logits of any grammar-violating token to -infinity before sampling
It filters the completed output text after generation
questions.explanation: The constraint is applied during decoding, at the logit level: at every step, the current automaton state determines which tokens are legal, and everything else gets masked to -infinity before the softmax and sample — invalid tokens simply can't be picked.

questions.prompt: What's a documented pitfall of constrained decoding?
options: It cannot produce valid JSON at all
It's slower than fine-tuning by several orders of magnitude with no benefit
Forcing structure too early can lock in an answer before the model has reasoned it through
It only works with proprietary APIs
questions.explanation: Because the grammar restricts every token from the very first one, applying it to a chain-of-thought stream (instead of just the final structured answer) can force a shape onto reasoning before the model has actually worked out the answer — best practice is to reason freely, then constrain only the final output.
